en/disconnected/index.title: Desconectado
en/disconnected/index.content:
SOLE Voltaje Disconnected
In 2024, the SOLE Colombia team designed a prototype so that anyone, anywhere in the world, regardless of prior knowledge, could understand how the internet works without the internet in a practical and fun way. This prototype is called Disconnected. After several tests, we developed this card game that invites us to navigate through stories, lessons, and very valuable information. Once you have explored this game, we believe you will be ready to identify how good your internet signal is, how it works, and you will be able to evaluate the best solutions for any connectivity problem you may have.
The interesting thing about this card game is that it can be expanded as much as we want. This means that we will be designing and expanding the cards in this game based on the lessons and contributions of the communities we work with.
This game is divided into 3 types of cards:

Cacharreras Cards (Tinkering Cards)
Navegadoras Cards (Navigating Cards)
Conectivas Cards (Connecting Cards)

This game has no specific order, so you can start with any of the three types of cards. Let’s get started!
Download the Disconnected card game here
Instructions for playing SOLE Voltaje Disconnected
Cacharreras Cards: How is your signal?
To understand how the internet works wherever you are in the world, you can start by tinkering with the signal you have. But what signal do you have? How does it work? We have two cards that will help you answer these questions in practice: how to tinker with your mobile signal? or how to tinker with your WiFi signal? This first distinction will allow you to distinguish how the internet signal reaches any device. Open either of the two cards and follow the instructions to start navigating.
Untitled
Navegadoras Cards: What would you like more?
These cards will help you navigate the internet while learning about the importance of asking Big Questions. You will also learn about how the internet travels, how fast it is, what signal you have, how to take advantage of it, and much more. To play this game, you can follow these steps:

Choose 2 random cards and place the “What would you like more?” card in the middle.
Answer what you would like more: Which of the two cards do you prefer? To be an “inter” traveling through a cable across the earth and oceans, or to travel at the speed of light? Combine the cards however you wish.
Flip the card you chose, read what it says, and solve the challenges that appear there. It is very likely that you will read cards that are connected to others. You can navigate as deep as you want.
If you are with friends, family, or acquaintances, you can do several rounds in which each person answers and shares what they would like more, reading the information and solving the challenges there as a team. We invite you to make whatever variations of this game you like best.

Conectivas Cards: What do you want to do?
These cards will show you different connectivity solutions that you can find on this Disconnected page. You can open any card, follow the instructions, and you will recognize whether that solution works for what you want to learn or solve. These cards are “connective” because they will lead you to find solutions to connect to the internet.
Depending on the connectivity problems or learning interests you have, you will find three types of cards for this category:

Solutions to get the internet
Solutions to improve the internet
Solutions to share the internet

What are the differences between these cards? We invite you to open any of them to find out.
Do you want to take a SOLE Voltaje solution to a real disconnected context?
In all the Inspirations and Solutions, you can download the material in PDF format. Print the material or copy it to a USB drive, and you can take it to places where you don’t have connectivity to try to solve their problems.
What are the connectivity challenges?
SOLE Voltaje was imagined for people with diverse connectivity challenges. After a survey we conducted in 2020 at SOLE Colombia, we discovered that half of the people we interacted with did not have the Internet for the following 4 reasons:

There is no signal: In the places where they live, there is no coverage for either mobile signal or cable signal. In some places, especially scattered rural areas, there are public schools with satellite internet connectivity provided by the government, but its quality and consistency are difficult to establish.
The signal is bad: In other places, the signal is intermittent. It did not allow them to make a video call or watch a streaming video. Usually, it required them to have to move around their territory to locate the best possibility to connect.
They don’t have money to pay for it: There might be a mobile or cable signal, however, it represents a very high cost for their personal or family expenses.
They don’t know what the Internet is for: Many people argue that they don’t have the Internet for any of the above reasons, but it can also be inferred that many people don’t know what the Internet is for, as they are willing to pay for other services like satellite TV instead of the Internet. In many communities, it is believed that the Internet is Facebook and WhatsApp, as that is what comes free with their mobile phone plan.

Everything starts with a Big Question

en/glossary/conc-2g-net.title: Red 2G
en/glossary/conc-2g-net.content:
The 2G (Second Generation) network is the mobile technology that marked the transition from analog to digital, making encrypted voice calls and text messages (SMS) possible. It serves for basic voice and text communications, in addition to supporting some limited data services such as email and low-speed internet access. It was fundamental to the global expansion of mobile telephony and the foundation for later technologies, although its data speed is low.
What is the 2G network?

Digitalization of communications: 2G was the first generation to adopt digital technology for mobile communications, replacing previous analog systems.
GSM technology: It is based on the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM).
Main services: Its primary function is voice call service and the sending and receiving of text messages (SMS).

What is it used for?

Voice calls: It allowed for encrypted voice calls with better quality than in the analog generation.
SMS messaging: It made it possible to send and receive text messages, which revolutionized the way people communicate.
Limited data services: With the introduction of services like GPRS (General Packet Radio Service) →, it opened the door to basic data services, allowing for very limited internet access and email.
Coverage: It is important because it provides good coverage in rural or mountainous areas where more advanced networks have not yet reached.
IoT (Internet of Things) devices: It continues to be used in some machine-to-machine (M2M) communication devices and GPS tracking devices.

Its legacy and future

Foundation for the future: 2G laid the groundwork for more advanced technologies like 3G and 4G by demonstrating the efficiency of the digital system.
Gradual shutdown: Due to its low data speed compared to newer generations, most operators are shutting down and replacing 2G networks to reallocate those frequencies to more efficient technologies like 4G and 5G.

Referencias | References

Wikipedia
WideTech
WirelessLogic
Lenovo

en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.title: Antena 3G/4G
en/glossary/conc-3g-4g-antennas.content:
A 3/4G antenna, also known as an LTE antenna, is a device that facilitates internet connection through 4G and 3G mobile networks. These antennas allow for the reception and transmission of radio signals to connect smartphones, tablets, and modems to the cellular network, improving the quality and speed of the connection.
More details:

Functionality: 3/4G antennas act as bridges between devices and mobile phone towers, enabling wireless communication.
Types of antennas: There are different types of 3/4G antennas, such as directional ones, which focus in one direction for greater range, and omnidirectional ones, which cover a wider area.
Signal improvement: By using a 3/4G antenna, the received signal can be boosted, especially in areas with poor coverage or indoors.
Importance of orientation: The orientation of the antenna is crucial to obtain the best possible signal, ideally pointing towards the nearest mobile phone tower.
Connection to devices: 3/4G antennas connect to devices via coaxial cables → and SMA connectors, or adapters if they are MIFI routers →.
MIMO technology: Some 4G antennas use MIMO (Multiple Input Multiple Output) technology, which employs multiple antennas to improve the speed and reliability of the connection.
Difference from WiFi: Unlike WiFi antennas → that operate in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, 4G antennas use different frequency bands defined by the operator.
Use in rural areas: In rural areas, where the signal may be weak, outdoor antennas can be especially useful for improving the internet connection.

en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.title: Ayudante Sabio (IA Local)
en/glossary/conc-ai-helper.content:
The Wise Assistant is a special Artificial Intelligence program that lives and works inside your own computer or server →. Unlike other AIs, it does not need the internet because everything it knows comes from the files and “digital books” that you save in its memory yourself.
In our technological kitchen:

It is an Expert Consultant.
It is not the one doing the physical work (that is done by the Processor or Cook →), but rather someone who analyzes the recipes and gives you advice.
Internal reading: The assistant does not go out into the street to look for answers; it reads the manuals, guides, and documents you have in the pantry (Storage →). That is why it is safe and private: what is discussed in the kitchen, stays in the kitchen.


The importance of the Countertop (RAM)
Although the assistant is very intelligent, it has a limitation: to be able to think and respond, it needs to spread all the information out on the Work Countertop (RAM Memory →).

If you have a lot of RAM (a large countertop), the assistant can read many pages at once and answer you quickly.
If you have very little RAM (a small countertop), the assistant has to keep opening and closing folders constantly, which makes it take a long time to give you an answer.


In summary: The assistant is only as agile as the space you give it to work on the countertop and how many of the cook’s assistants help it.


What is it for?

Analyze your own data: You can ask it to summarize meeting minutes from the village or help you find a date in a long document.
Educational support: It helps students understand difficult concepts by explaining them in simple words.
Translation and writing: It helps translate texts from one language to another or write formal letters for the community.

en/glossary/conc-antenna.title: Antena
en/glossary/conc-antenna.content:
Briefly, an antenna is a device designed to transmit and/or receive electromagnetic waves.
About antennas


Transmission: Antennas emit electromagnetic waves into space, enabling long-distance communication. Nasa


Reception: They can also receive electromagnetic waves, transforming them into electrical signals that can be processed by a receiver. Invisible pillars of wireless communication


Types of antennas: There are various types of antennas, such as parabolic antennas, dipoles, and Yagi antennas →, each with specific characteristics for different applications. Types of antennas


Applications: Antennas are essential in broadcasting, television, mobile communications →, wireless networks → and many other technologies that use electromagnetic waves. Vicente Miralles Segarra Telecommunications Museum




References

Nasa
Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.title: Ancho de Banda
en/glossary/conc-bandwidth.content:
Bandwidth is the capacity of a network connection to transport data. It is usually measured in Megabits per second (Mbps).
In our technological kitchen:

It is the Size of the Hallway that leads to the kitchen.
If the hallway is narrow, only one person can pass at a time with their plate; if there are many people, they crowd together and everyone arrives late to the table.
If the hallway is wide, many people can enter and exit with a lot of food at the same time smoothly.


Don’t confuse it with speed
Many people believe that bandwidth is speed, but in reality, it is capacity. A wide hallway doesn’t make you walk faster, but it does allow more people to walk together without slowing down. The more bandwidth your community has, the more neighbors will be able to use the server at the same time without it getting slow.

en/glossary/conc-canva.title: Canva
en/glossary/conc-canva.content:
Canva is a free online graphic design platform that allows anyone, with or without design experience, to create various types of professional designs.
It offers a simple and intuitive interface with a wide range of templates, images, fonts, and graphic elements to facilitate the creation of presentations, social media posts, infographics, cards, resumes, and much more.

en/glossary/conc-client.title: Cliente
en/glossary/conc-client.content:
In computing, a client is a piece of hardware or software that accesses a service or resource provided by a server →.
The term can refer to both a physical device (such as a computer or smartphone) and a software program (such as a web browser) used to interact with a server. (Source: Brave)
More about “clients”


Client role: The client sends requests to the server to access data, services, or resources that it provides. (Source: IONOS)


Client-server interaction: In a client-server architecture, the client initiates communication and the server → responds to the client’s requests. (Source: IONOS)


Examples:

A web browser like Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox is a client that requests web pages from a server. (Source: Brave)
An email program that connects to a server to send and receive messages is another example. (Source: Linube)
A mobile device that accesses a cloud application is another example of a client. (Source: TechTarget)

Types of clients:

Thick clients: Have local storage capacity and can run applications independently. (Source: Slideshare)
Thin clients: Rely primarily on the server for application execution and data storage. (Source: Slideshare)

Why are they important?
Clients allow users to access a wide range of services and resources remotely, facilitating interaction with distributed systems and networks. (Source: Oracle)

en/glossary/conc-coaxial-cable.title: Cable coaxial
en/glossary/conc-coaxial-cable.content:
The coaxial cable is a cable used to transport high-frequency electrical signals.
It has two concentric conductors:

the central one, called the core: responsible for carrying information
the outer one, tubular in appearance, called the mesh, shield, or braid: serves as a ground reference and return for currents.

Between the two, there is an insulating dielectric layer, the characteristics of which will mainly determine the quality of the cable.
The entire assembly is usually protected by an insulating sheath (also called an outer jacket).

💡 Parts of the RG-59 coaxial cable (for signals). See also: RG6 Cable →
A: plastic protective sheath (thermoplastic elastomer)
B: copper mesh (shielded conductor made of copper-clad aluminum braid)
C: insulator (foam dielectric)
D: central conductor or copper core (copper-clad steel).
References:
A coaxial cable consists of electronic signals that constitute the information Wikipedia.gov

en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.title: Símbolo de sistema CMD
en/glossary/conc-command-prompt.content:
In the context of Windows, CMD, or Command Prompt, it is a command-line interface that allows you to interact with the operating system → using text commands.
It is a useful tool for executing commands, managing files, troubleshooting, and automating tasks.
The Command Prompt (CMD) is:

A command interpreter: CMD takes commands written by the user and translates them into actions that the operating system can understand and execute.
An alternative to the graphical interface: Although Windows has a graphical interface, CMD offers a faster and more efficient way to perform certain tasks, especially for advanced users or for automating processes.
A troubleshooting tool: CMD allows you to run commands to diagnose and fix system problems, such as network errors or configuration issues.
A base for scripts: CMD is the foundation for creating and running scripts, which allows for the automation of repetitive and complex tasks.

In summary, CMD is an essential tool for the management and administration of Windows systems, offering a powerful and flexible way to interact with the operating system using text commands.

en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.title: Procesador (CPU)
en/glossary/conc-cpu-processor.content:
The Processor or CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the component that performs calculations and makes decisions in your computer.
In our technological kitchen:

The Processor is The Chef.
It is the one who takes the ingredients on the counter (RAM Memory →), reads the recipe (the program), and prepares the final result.
The speed of the chef (measured in Gigahertz or GHz) defines how fast information is processed or how quickly it cooks things.


Why does it matter?
A chef can have “several arms” (called Cores). If it has 4 cores, it is as if you had 4 chefs working at the same time on different dishes. This is what allows your computer to do several things at once without freezing.

Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-daemon.title: Demonio (servicio o programa)
en/glossary/conc-daemon.content:
A service, resident program, or daemon is a special type of program that runs in the background, rather than being directly controlled by the user. These types of programs remain in the system, meaning they can run persistently or restart if an attempt is made to “kill” the process, depending on the daemon’s configuration and system policies. The use of this name comes from the backronym Daemon (Disk And Execution Monitor).
Daemons usually have the following characteristics:

They do not have a direct “interface” with the user, neither graphical nor textual.
They do not use standard input and output to report errors or log their operation; instead, they use system files in special areas (/var/log/ in most modern UNIX systems) or use other daemons specialized in such logging, like syslogd.

For example, a machine hosting a web server → will use an HTTP daemon to provide the service so that visitors to said web page can access it. Another example is “chronological” daemons like cron, which perform scheduled tasks such as system maintenance in the background.

en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.title: Protocolo DHCP
en/glossary/conc-dhcp-protocol.content:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is the service responsible for assigning IP addresses automatically.
In our technological kitchen:

DHCP is The Receptionist.
When someone arrives at the kitchen (connects to the WiFi), the Receptionist greets them and says: “Welcome, today you will identify yourself with the number 15 (IP 192.168.1.15)“.
Thanks to the Receptionist, you don’t have to configure anything manually on your phone; they ensure everyone has a name and a place at the table.


Why is it useful?
DHCP allows devices to request and receive an IP address from a DHCP server, simplifying network administration and avoiding IP address conflicts. (Sources: Akamai and Arsys)
Imagine that 20 people arrive at a community meeting with their phones. Without a Receptionist (DHCP), you would have to go one by one assigning numbers so they don’t repeat. DHCP does it in milliseconds.

Related concepts

en/glossary/conc-dns.title: DNS (Sistema de Nombres de Dominio)
en/glossary/conc-dns.content:
DNS is like a massive address book that associates a domain name (like google.com) with a numerical address (IP →). (Sources: Cloudflare and Wikipedia)
In our tech kitchen:

DNS is Nicknames.
Instead of telling the delivery person to go to “House 192.168.1.15”, we simply tell them to go to where “David” is or to the “Community Kitchen”.
The nickname system is much easier for people to remember, but the system knows which numerical address corresponds to each nickname.


How does it work?
When you type a domain name into your browser, it sends a request to a DNS server. The server looks for the corresponding IP address and returns it to the browser so that it can connect to the web server hosting the site.
On your Pocket Server →, we set up a local nickname like solevoltaje.local. This way, any neighbor who connects to your WiFi only has to type that name into their browser to enter the “Community Kitchen”, without having to learn difficult numbers.

en/glossary/conc-dnsmasq.title: Redireccionador DNS y servidor DHCP ligero
en/glossary/conc-dnsmasq.content:
Dnsmasq is software that provides Domain Name System (DNS) caching, Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP →) server, router advertisement, and network boot functions for small computer networks, created as free software.
Dnsmasq has low system resource requirements, can run on Linux, BSD, Android, and macOS, and is included in most Linux distributions.
Consequently, “it is present in many home routers → and certain gadgets for the Internet of Things,” and it is also included in Android.
If you want to know more details, you can consult Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-docker-container.title: Contenedores Docker
en/glossary/conc-docker-container.content:
Docker is a technology that allows you to “package” an application along with everything it needs to run (such as languages, databases, and configurations) inside a box called a Container.
In our kitchen analogy:

Docker is a pre-equipped portable kitchen.
Imagine you want to set up a restaurant on another street. Instead of bringing bricks, pots, and hiring a plumber, you bring a container that already has the stove installed, the pots in their place, and the recipes ready. You just plug it in and that’s it!
This ensures that if an application (like a digital library) works on my computer, it will work exactly the same on your Raspberry Pi or the school server.


What is it for?
In community projects, Docker is a blessing because it allows you to share complex systems (like a file server or a local AI) “hand-in-hand.” You just pass the “container” and the other person doesn’t have to struggle with difficult installations; everything starts up on the first try.

en/glossary/conc-domain-name.title: Nombre de dominio
en/glossary/conc-domain-name.content:
A domain name is a unique, easy-to-remember address used to access a website or an internet service.
It is like a website’s postal address, but instead of numbers, it uses text. For example, “solecolombia.org” is a domain name. It allows users to access websites and services without having to remember complex IP addresses →. (Source: Google Help)
In more technical terms, a domain name is a way to translate a numerical IP address (such as 192.0.2.1) into a string of text that is easy to remember and type, such as “example.com”. This translation process is performed by the Domain Name System (DNS) →, which is a directory that associates domain names with their corresponding IP addresses.
Here are some key points about domain names:

Ease of use: Domain names make it much easier for people to find and access websites, as they are easier to remember and type than IP addresses.
Online identity: A domain name is essentially the identity of a website or service on the internet. It is what users will type into their browser to visit your site.
Ownership and registration: Domain names are registered with authorized registrars and paid for annually to maintain ownership.
Components of a domain: A domain name typically consists of two main parts: the name (e.g., “solecolombia”) and the extension or top-level domain (e.g., “.org”).

A domain name is an essential tool for internet navigation, allowing users to access websites and services easily and efficiently, and it also serves as a website’s identity on the web.

en/glossary/conc-edge-connection.title: Conexión EDGE
en/glossary/conc-edge-connection.content:
The EDGE connection related to Mobile telephony technology refers to the “Enhanced Data rates for GSM of Evolution” (EDGE) mobile technology, a 2G network that acts as a bridge to 3G to offer basic internet, or to the concept of “Edge Computing,” a method of processing data near its source to speed up high-speed applications and services on connected devices, such as the Internet of Things (IoT).
It is an evolution of GPRS → that improves data transfer speeds on 2G mobile networks →, serving as an intermediate step toward 3G networks.
It allows for a faster data connection than 2G, suitable for basic tasks such as video calls, sending messages, and web browsing, before the arrival of 3G networks. The “E” symbol on a phone indicates that it is connected to this network.

en/glossary/conc-ethernet.title: Conexión/cable Ethernet
en/glossary/conc-ethernet.content:
An Ethernet connection is a technology that allows electronic devices to be connected to a local area network (LAN) → or a wide area network (WAN) using a cable. Its main function is the transmission of data between devices, whether to share information or to connect to the internet.
In more detail:

Wired connection: Ethernet uses cables, generally RJ45 cables, to establish communication between devices. There are different types of Ethernet cables, categorized by their transfer speed and network frequency. Ethernet offers faster speeds and a more stable connection than wireless connections, such as Wi-Fi →, in addition to being more secure and economical.
Connects devices: Ethernet is used to connect a wide variety of devices, including computers, routers, video game consoles, smart TVs, and more. It is the most common technology for connecting devices within the same area, such as an office or a home.
Transmits data: Through Ethernet cables, devices can send and receive data packets, allowing for communication and the exchange of information.
Comparison with Wi-Fi: Although Wi-Fi is more convenient, Ethernet offers a better experience in terms of speed, stability, and security.

In summary, an Ethernet connection is a fundamental technology for wired data networks, providing a reliable and efficient way to connect devices and share information.

en/glossary/conc-firewall.title: Firewall (Cortafuegos)
en/glossary/conc-firewall.content:
A Firewall is a security tool that monitors network traffic and decides whether to allow or block the passage of information based on defined rules.
In our technological kitchen:

The Firewall is The Doorman.
It stands at the kitchen door watching every ingredient and every person trying to enter.
If someone tries to bring in something rotten (a virus) or enter uninvited (an attack), the doorman blocks their path to protect the cook and the diners.


Why is it important?
In a community network, the Firewall ensures that outsiders cannot access neighbors’ private information or damage the operation of the Pocket Server →. It is like having a smart lock on the kitchen door.

en/glossary/conc-firmware.title: Firmware
en/glossary/conc-firmware.content:
Firmware is a type of computer program that provides low-level control for a device’s specific hardware. It sits “in the middle” between hardware and software.
In our tech kitchen:

Firmware is The Stove Manual.
It is the factory-recorded instructions that tell the stove how to ignite when you turn the knob, or the router how its lights should blink.


Why is it important?
Sometimes equipment needs a “firmware update.” It is as if the manufacturer sent a new page for the stove manual so that it uses less gas or is safer. Keeping it up to date helps your pocket server be more stable.

Related concepts

Hardware →
Operating System →

en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.title: Memoria USB
en/glossary/conc-flashdrive-usb.content:
The USB Flash Drive (also known as a “pendrive” or “thumb drive”) is a small storage device that connects to a computer via a USB → port.
In our kitchen analogy:

The USB flash drive is like a lunchbox or a small container.
It is used to carry a portion of food (your files) from one kitchen (computer) to another, without having to move the entire pantry (Hard Drive →).


A bit of history
USB flash drives appeared in the late 90s and replaced floppy disks and CDs. Previously, to save a single song or document, you needed a square, noisy disk that was easily damaged.
The USB flash drive revolutionized everything because it is small, durable, and does not need batteries or extra cables. Its capacity has grown immensely: today, a USB flash drive the size of a finger can store thousands of books or hundreds of movies.

What is it used for?

Carrying files: Documents, photos, or music.
Backing up information: Having a backup copy outside of the computer.
Installing programs: It is often used to install an Operating System → (such as Windows or Linux) on a new computer.


Recommendation…

Attention: USB flash drives are very useful but easy to lose. Never store sensitive information (such as passwords) on them without protection. They are also one of the most common ways viruses are passed between computers; make sure to always scan them.

Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
SD Memory →

en/glossary/conc-gprs.title: GPRS (Servicio General de Paquetes Vía Radio)
en/glossary/conc-gprs.content:
GPRS was a key technology that introduced the concept of packet data transfer in mobile networks, laying the foundation for the mobile data services we take for granted today, and it remains useful in applications where data transfer does not require high speed.

General Packet Radio Service: It means that information is divided into small “packets” of data, which are sent independently across the network.
GPRS is a data communication protocol that operates over second-generation (2G) mobile networks →, acting as an enhancement to GSM technology.
Instead of using a dedicated and continuous channel for data (like GSM), GPRS allocates network resources only when data is being sent, which makes it more efficient.

What is it used for?

Internet Access and Mobile Data: It allowed users to connect to the internet from their mobile devices, albeit at moderate speeds.
Multimedia Messaging (MMS) and Email: It facilitated the sending and receiving of more complex messages than SMS.
Location Services: It was used to provide location services through the mobile network.
Security Alarms: GPRS remains relevant in alarm systems, as it allows for the secure transmission of alarm signals without relying on a fixed telephone line.

en/glossary/conc-hardware.title: Hardware
en/glossary/conc-hardware.content:
Hardware refers to all the physical components of a computer system. They are the pieces of metal, plastic, and circuits that give the equipment its body.
In our technological kitchen:

Hardware is The Utensils and Furniture.
The pot (the computer), the burners (the processor), the countertop (the RAM), and the shelves (the hard drive).
Without hardware, the software (Operating System →) would have nowhere to “cook” anything.


Why does care matter?
Just as if a pot gets burned or bent it stops working well, if the hardware is hit, gets wet, or overheats, the system will fail even if the recipes (the software) are perfect. Keeping the hardware clean and cool is key for your pocket server to last for many years.

Related concepts

Software (Operating System) →
Processor (CPU) →
RAM Memory →


Change history















DateChangeAuthor2026-04-05Initial version publishedDavid

en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.title: Demonio Hostapd
en/glossary/conc-hostapd-daemon.content:
A Hostapd (host access point daemon) is a user-space daemon that allows a network interface card (NIC) to function as a wireless access point (AP) and an authentication server.
In essence, it turns your computer into a Wi-Fi → router, allowing other devices to connect to the internet through it.
In more detail:

Access Point (AP): Hostapd creates a wireless network that other devices can connect to, similar to a traditional router.
Authentication Server: It manages the authentication of users attempting to connect to the network, ensuring that only authorized devices can gain access.
IEEE 802.11: Hostapd implements the IEEE 802.11 protocol, the standard for wireless networks, which includes features such as access point management, authentication (WPA/WPA2), and access to protected networks.
Implementations: There are several hostapd implementations, such as the one by Jouni Malinen (the most common), OpenBSD, and Devicescape.
Linux and FreeBSD: Hostapd is compatible with Linux (Host AP, madwifi, and mac80211-based drivers) and FreeBSD (net80211).
Common use: It is mainly used on devices like Raspberry Pi to create Wi-Fi access points and in wireless security testing systems.

en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.title: Tecnología HSPA (Acceso de Paquetes de Alta Velocidad)
en/glossary/conc-hspa-technology.content:
HSPA stands for “High-Speed Packet Access” and is an enhancement technology for 3G mobile networks that increases the speed and efficiency of data transfer, both for downloading (HSDPA) and uploading (HSUPA).
It serves to allow mobile devices to access the internet at speeds higher than basic 3G networks, facilitating access to faster data services on smartphones → and tablets, especially in areas where 4G or 5G are not available.
What is HSPA?

HSPA is a third-generation (3G) technology that improves UMTS and WCDMA networks, incorporating HSDPA technologies for downlink and HSUPA for uplink.
HSDPA (High-Speed Downlink Packet Access): Improves data download speed, allowing for faster browsing and access to heavy content.
HSUPA (High-Speed Uplink Packet Access): Increases data upload speed, which facilitates the uploading of photos, videos, and other large files to the network.

What is HSPA used for?

Higher data speed: HSPA offers significantly higher data speeds compared to initial 3G networks, making an experience similar to DSL connections possible.
Improved network efficiency: It uses techniques such as advanced modulation and greater spectrum utilization to transmit data more efficiently.
Access to data services: It allows mobile devices to access high-speed data services, such as web browsing, video streaming, and application downloads, more smoothly.
Support for multiple simultaneous services: With 3G and HSPA technology, mobile devices can maintain voice calls and data services at the same time.
Connection in areas with poor coverage: Although 4G and 5G networks are present, HSPA remains relevant and is crucial for maintaining connectivity in rural areas or when 4G coverage is limited or experiences congestion.

en/glossary/conc-imei-code.title: Código IMEI
en/glossary/conc-imei-code.content:
The IMEI is a unique 15-digit code that identifies every mobile phone worldwide. It stands for “International Mobile Equipment Identity” and serves to identify a specific device, like an ID card for cell phones, allowing carriers to distinguish it on their networks. (Source: BBVA)

Unique identification: The IMEI is a unique serial number for each phone, which allows it to be distinguished from any other device. (Source: Enacom)
Network information: Carriers use it to identify the device when it connects to the network, allowing for the tracking, locking, and unlocking of the phone. (Source:BBVA)
Security and control: The IMEI is used to report stolen or lost phones and block them, preventing them from being used with other SIM cards. (Source:BBC)
How to find it? You can find your phone’s IMEI by dialing *#06# on the keypad or by checking the device settings, the original box, or under the battery. (Source:T-Mobile)
Utility: In addition to security, the IMEI can be useful for obtaining information about the device, such as the model, brand, and country of origin.


  
  

It is not the same as the SIM: Unlike the SIM card →, which can be moved from one phone to another, the IMEI is a unique identifier for the device itself.

en/glossary/conc-information-system.title: Sistema informático (SI)
en/glossary/conc-information-system.content:
We understand a computer system as the set of physical and logical elements responsible for receiving, storing, and processing data to then deliver it in the form of results. The scheme of a computer system encompasses everything that contains a tangible part (hardware →) and a logical part (software →).
Currently, CSs occupy a key place in human organization, as they turn out to be a powerful tool for the exchange of information and the development of computer networks that overcome the barrier of distance.
Components of a computer system
The elements that form the basic structure of every computer system are:

Hardware: includes all the physical parts of the CS, that is, everything that can be touched. In the case of a computer, these elements of the computer system would be: the screen, the keyboard, or the mouse.
Software: refers to the logical part of every computer system, the intangible. It is the set of programs including data, instructions, applications, etc., that allow the user to communicate with the hardware to perform various tasks.
Computer personnel: any person who uses the system in some way, including software creators, programmers, or users in general.

Characteristics of a computer system
Some characteristics that define a CS are:

Computer systems are designed to process, store, obtain, and receive information.
They provide a user-friendly interface for use and management by people.
They facilitate the automation of processes, since the programming of a computer system is aimed at performing tasks autonomously.
Their primary objective is to offer new and better living conditions to human beings.

Classification of computer systems
Computer systems can be classified according to their:

Processing volume: depending on the capacity they have to process and manage data.
Utilization: that is, the use given to the computer system, whether to fulfill tasks with reduced criteria or to handle a greater number of variables.
Function: depending on whether it is designed to fulfill specific purposes within a series of jobs. It could be programmed to provide suggestions for decision-making or to make a decision on its own based on collected data.
Grouping: depending on whether they are isolated systems or part of networks of equipment interconnected in private, local, wide networks, etc.

Once we understand what computer systems are, we move on to name some practical applications, that is, what a computer system is used for in the real world. (Source: Universidad Isabel I)

en/glossary/conc-interface.title: Interfaz
en/glossary/conc-interface.content:
Generally speaking, an interface is a point of contact or connection between two systems, components, or entities that allows for interaction and the exchange of information between them.
It can be physical, such as the connection between a keyboard and a computer, or logical, such as the way a program communicates with the operating system →.
Types of interfaces:

User Interface (UI): This is the way a user interacts with a system, whether it is a program, a webpage, or a device. It includes visual and functional elements that allow the user to perform actions and navigate the system. (Source: Wikipedia)
Application Programming Interface (API): Defines how different programs or software components can communicate with each other, allowing the functions and data of other programs to be used. (Source: Microsoft)
Network Interface: This is the connection point between devices on a network, such as a network interface card (NIC) that connects a computer to a network. (Source: Microsoft)
Brain-Computer Interface (BCI): This is an innovative technology that allows for direct communication between the brain and an external device, such as a prosthesis. (Source: Wikipedia)

In summary, an interface facilitates interaction and the exchange of information between different parts, whether they are physical, logical, or conceptual.
Wireless interfaces
A wireless interface is a mechanism that allows communication between electronic devices without the need for physical cables, using radio waves or other wireless technologies. It allows for connection to computer networks, such as Wi-Fi, or communication between nearby devices, such as Bluetooth.
In more detail:

Wireless communication: Unlike wired interfaces, which require physical connections like Ethernet or USB cables, wireless interfaces use radio waves or other technologies to transmit data. (Source: Mastervolt)
Common types: The most common examples of wireless interfaces include Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11), Bluetooth, and NFC. (Source: Fibermall)
Functionality: These interfaces are usually integrated into wireless network interface cards (WNICs) or adapters, which connect to devices and allow communication with other devices or networks via radio waves. (Source: Quora)
Applications: Wireless interfaces are fundamental for the connectivity of mobile devices, such as laptops, smartphones, and tablets, and for the creation of wireless local area networks (WLAN or Wi-Fi). (Source: Cisco)
Security: Wireless interfaces usually include security mechanisms, such as WPA3, to protect the information being transmitted. (Source: Fibermall)
Operating modes: Some wireless network cards can function as access points (APs) for other devices to connect to, or as clients that access a network through an access point. (Source: Vyos)

en/glossary/conc-ip-address.title: Dirección IP
en/glossary/conc-ip-address.content:
An IP Address (Internet Protocol) is a series of numbers that identifies a device (computer, cell phone, printer) on a network.
In our technological kitchen:

The IP is the House Address.
For data to reach where it needs to go, every device needs a unique address. For example, on your local network, addresses usually start with 192.168.1....
Without this address, the Delivery Person (Nginx) → wouldn’t know which screen to deliver the information to.


Local IP vs. Public IP

Local IP: It is your device’s address inside your home or neighborhood. It is like the internal room number in a hotel.
Public IP: It is your network’s address to the outside world (the vast internet). It is like the main address of the hotel in the city.

en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.title: Lenguaje JavaScript
en/glossary/conc-javascript-language.content:
JavaScript (JS) is the language that brings to life what you see in your browser or on your phone.
In our tech kitchen:

JavaScript is the dynamic waiter.
While HTML sets the table and CSS chooses the color of the tablecloth, JavaScript is the one that makes the menu change when you swipe, notifies you when your order is ready, or allows you to chat with others without reloading the page.
Unlike PHP or Python, which usually work “inside” the kitchen (the server), JavaScript usually works “outside” with the client (on your phone).


Why is it important?
Without JavaScript, the internet would be a series of static pages like old newspapers. Thanks to JS, we can have applications on the local server that feel fast and modern, allowing the community to interact fluidly.

Related concepts

PHP Language →
Python Language →

en/glossary/conc-latency.title: Latencia
en/glossary/conc-latency.content:
Latency is the exact time it takes for a data packet to be transmitted over a network.
It is the time that elapses from when your browser makes a request for information to the time it takes for the requested response to arrive.
The lower the latency, the better the internet connection.
To calculate latency, two parameters are used: the ping →, a unit of measurement expressed in milliseconds (ms), and lag, which refers to excessive delay.
You can measure both parameters with a speed test.
What is ping?
Ping is a unit of measurement used to measure latency. Before continuing, do you know what latency consists of? In simple terms, latency is the time it takes for a data packet to be transmitted within the network. That is, it is the exact time that passes from when your device made a request to the server to the time it takes to receive a response from the server.
On the other hand, ping is the metric used to measure latency and is expressed in milliseconds (or its abbreviation ms). This means that the lower the ping, the better. It is recommended that the ping be below 100 ms; from 65 ms onwards, the connection is sufficient, and you should not experience any issues with video calls. If you are a gamer, the most optimal ping would be around 20 ms so that you do not have much delay or lag.
What is lag?
Lag refers to the excessive delay that can be caused by real-time telecommunication. Its causes can be related to high network latency or because there is not enough processing power in the service or client with which the communication is established. It could be your computer or the internet connection.
Lag occurs depending on the format in which it is presented. For example, in videos, the image usually worsens, your music may have sound with interference, and the classic one in online video games: the delay in your character performing your commands.

en/glossary/conc-linux-system.title: Sistema Linux
en/glossary/conc-linux-system.content:
Linux is an open-source operating system, which means its original “recipe” is public and anyone can view, copy, or improve it.
In our technological kitchen:

Linux is a Modular and Free Kitchen.
Unlike other kitchens where you cannot change anything, in Linux you can move the counters, change the color of the walls, and even invent new ways of cooking.
It is famous for being very secure and stable: once you turn on the stove in a Linux kitchen, it can run for years without shutting down.


Why do we use it at Voltaje?
We use Linux because it doesn’t charge us to use it, it respects our privacy, and it works very well on old equipment that other systems already consider “trash.” It is the solid ground upon which we build our Pocket Internet →.

en/glossary/conc-local-network.title: LAN (Red local)
en/glossary/conc-local-network.content:
A local area network, or LAN, is a group of devices (such as computers, phones, printers, etc.) connected to each other in a limited geographical area, such as a home, an office, or a building.
These networks allow devices to share resources such as files, printers, and an Internet connection. (Source: Cloudflare)
Main characteristics of a LAN:

Limited coverage: LANs are designed for small geographical areas. (Source: NinjaOne)
Connection of nearby devices: Devices connect to each other via cables → or wireless connections → within a delimited physical space. (Source: Share.google)
Resource sharing: Devices on a LAN can access and share files, printers, and other resources. (Source: Servicios UNS)
Shared Internet connection: A LAN can share a single Internet connection among multiple devices. (Source: Cloudflare)
Control and security: LANs allow for centralized management of security and access to shared resources. (Source: AWS)
Speed: LANs typically offer faster data transfer speeds than larger networks. (Source: Coltecno)

Examples of LANs:

A home network that connects computers, smartphones, and other devices in a house.
An office network that connects employee computers and printers.
A school network that connects student and teacher computers.

(Source: OliviaWireless)
In summary, a LAN is a computer network that allows communication and resource sharing between devices in a local area. (Source: Share.google)

en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.title: Conexión 4G o LTE
en/glossary/conc-lte-4g-connection.content:
LTE, an acronym for Long Term Evolution, is a global wireless communication standard that provides fourth-generation (4G) mobile network technology, offering much faster data transfer speeds and reduced latency → compared to the previous generation (3G). Its main function is to enable high-speed internet access on mobile devices, enabling services such as video streaming, fast content downloading, and IoT (Internet of Things) applications.
What is LTE used for?


Web browsing and content streaming: Allows for faster and smoother downloading of websites, videos, and music.


High-quality calls: Voice over LTE (VoLTE) technology allows voice calls to be made over the LTE data network, improving sound quality and reducing call setup time.


Improved mobile device communication: Facilitates more efficient instant messaging and video communication.


Expansion of IoT applications: LTE is fundamental for connecting a large number of devices, such as smartwatches, sensors, and automation systems, to the internet.


Telecommuting and remote work: Allows for video conferencing and access to cloud platforms with greater stability and speed, making it possible to work from anywhere.


Standardization and evolution:
LTE is a long-term standard that remains the foundation for 5G mobile networks and will continue to evolve with variants such as LTE-Advanced (LTE-A) to offer even higher speeds and performance.

en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.title: Módem MiFi
en/glossary/conc-mifi-modem.content:
A MiFi modem, also known as a portable WiFi router, is a device that allows you to create a local WiFi network using a mobile data connection, such as 4G or 5G, so that multiple devices can access the internet wirelessly. Essentially, it is a portable WiFi hotspot that you can carry with you. (Source: Verizon)
The MiFi establishes high-speed broadband connectivity that can be shared by up to ten users at a time. It can be used with multiple WiFi devices such as: desktop computers, laptops, tablets, mobile phones, cameras, video game consoles, and MP3 players. In many cases, for example with the Apple iPad, it can replace having an internet connection inside the device, and you won’t need to pay for another service.
Additionally, some devices can be used as a USB flash drive since they have internal storage space and can even be expanded with memory cards.
When in use, devices connect to the MiFi network just like any other network. The achievable transfer speeds vary depending on the level of service and the type of network (for example, 3G or 4G) to which it is linked. (Source: Wikipedia)

en/glossary/conc-network-agents.title: Agentes de Red
en/glossary/conc-network-agents.content:
Network Agents are small programs or services (such as hostapd or dnsmasq) that handle automatic tasks to keep the network running.
In our tech kitchen:

They are The Link Helpers.
While the chef prepares the food, these helpers take care of things like: announcing that the kitchen is open, assigning turns at the entrance, or making sure the tables are clean and connected.


Which agents do we use?
In your Pocket Server →, we use agents like hostapd to create the WiFi and dnsmasq so that everyone gets an IP automatically. Without them, the network administrator would have to do all the heavy lifting by hand.

en/glossary/conc-nginx.title: Servidor Web Nginx (El Repartidor)
en/glossary/conc-nginx.content:
Nginx (pronounced “en-gine-ex”) is a program called a “Web Server.” Its main function is to receive requests from browsers (like Chrome or Firefox) and respond by sending the requested files.
In our tech kitchen:

Nginx is the Delivery Person.
When someone types an address from their phone, the Delivery Person runs to the kitchen, grabs the prepared dish (the webpage or file), and takes it to their screen.
It is very fast and can serve hundreds of people at the same time without getting tired.


Nicknames and Addresses
Since real addresses are long numbers that are hard to remember (called IPs), we use the DNS → system to give the delivery person nicknames.
Instead of telling neighbors to look for the delivery person at “Street 192.168.1.15,” we tell them: “Look for solevoltaje.local.” It is a familiar name that everyone can easily learn, just like we use nicknames for delivery apps or for friends in the neighborhood.

en/glossary/conc-operating-system.title: Sistema Operativo
en/glossary/conc-operating-system.content:
An Operating System (OS) is the main program that manages all the hardware and software of a computer or mobile phone.
In our technological kitchen:

The Operating System is the Design and Rules of the Kitchen.
It defines where the countertops are located (RAM), how to access the pantry (Hard Drive), and who has permission to use the knives (security).
It is responsible for ensuring the chef (processor) does not get confused and knows which order to attend to first.


Different kitchen styles
Each operating system has its own way of organizing things:

Windows: It is like a pre-fabricated and very popular kitchen. Everything comes in its place and it is easy to use for most, but sometimes it is heavy and difficult to modify.
macOS (Apple): It is a designer kitchen, very elegant and fluid, but it only works in the houses (equipment) that they build themselves.
Linux: It is a kitchen that you can assemble and modify to your liking. It is the foundation of almost all Servers → in the world.

Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-php-language.title: Lenguaje PHP
en/glossary/conc-php-language.content:
PHP is a programming language designed especially for creating websites and applications that run on a Server →.
In our community kitchen:

PHP is a specialized kitchen assistant.
While HTML is like the printed menu (which doesn’t change), PHP is the assistant who knows that if a customer orders “Sancocho,” they must go to the pantry, get the ingredients, and prepare it on the spot.
Thanks to PHP, the server can show different things to each person (for example, displaying your username or your personal files).


Why is it important?
PHP is the engine behind very famous tools like WordPress, Wikipedia (MediaWiki), or Facebook. In a local community network, installing PHP allows your server to stop being a simple list of files and become an interactive platform where people can publish their own stories or manage their documents.

en/glossary/conc-ping-program.title: Programa ping
en/glossary/conc-ping-program.content:
The ping program is a network diagnostic tool used to verify connectivity and latency between two devices.
In essence, ping sends a data packet to a target device and measures the time it takes to receive a response. This time, measured in milliseconds, is known as latency → or ping, and it is used to evaluate the quality of the connection.
How does it work?

The ping command sends an ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) packet to the target device.
The target device, if online, responds with an ICMP echo packet.
The ping tool measures the time it takes for the response to arrive and displays it as “round-trip time” (RTT) in milliseconds.
Additionally, ping can indicate if there is packet loss, which means that some packets did not reach their destination.

What is it used for?

Verifying connectivity: Ensuring that a device is connected and responding on the network.
Measuring latency: Determining the quality of the connection, especially in online gaming and video conferencing.
Diagnosing network problems: Identifying connectivity issues, packet loss, or high latency.

In summary, ping is an essential tool for diagnosing and evaluating the quality of the network connection between two devices.

en/glossary/conc-python-language.title: Lenguaje Python
en/glossary/conc-python-language.content:
Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world because it is very easy to read and can be used for almost anything.
In our tech kitchen:

Python is the Master Chef.
It is famous because its recipes read almost as if they were written in plain English.
It knows how to do everything: from automatically organizing the shopping list to training a “wise assistant” (Artificial Intelligence →).
It is the language most used to create AI Agents that can live inside your pocket server.


What is it used for?
In a community, Python is the ideal tool to automate processes, analyze weather or crop data, or run language models that help summarize important information without needing to connect to the internet.

Related concepts

JavaScript Language →
Local AI Possibilities →

en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.title: Memoria RAM
en/glossary/conc-ram-memory.content:
RAM (Random Access Memory) is the place where your computer stores the information it is using right at this moment.
To understand it easily, imagine your computer is a kitchen:

The RAM is the countertop.
The larger the countertop, the more ingredients (programs) you can have open and ready to chop without them falling to the floor or piling up.
The processor is the chef, who takes what they need from the countertop.


How does it work?
When you open a program (like a browser or a document), the computer takes it out of the “pantry” (the hard drive) and puts it on the “countertop” (the RAM).
The detail is that RAM is a kitchen assistant with a short-term memory: it is incredibly fast at handing you things, but as soon as you turn off the stove (the computer), it clears the countertop and forgets everything that was there. That is why, if you don’t “save” your work to the hard drive, it is lost.

Why is it important?
If you have a lot of RAM, you can have many pots on the stove and chop several ingredients at the same time. If you have very little, the chef has to keep putting things away in the pantry and taking them back out every time they are needed, which makes the whole lunch (your work) take much longer.

Related concepts

Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
Operating System →
Swap Memory →

en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.title: Raspberry Pi
en/glossary/conc-raspberry-pi.content:
What is it?
A Raspberry Pi is a credit card-sized computer that you can configure to your needs.
Initially, it does not have a keyboard, mouse, or monitor, but you can connect these and other peripherals to it without any problem.
Its “hard drive” is a MicroSD → memory card, on which a version of Linux → is installed, optimized for this type of device, which allows you to have a very portable computer that consumes few electricity resources, and on which you can do everything you normally do with a desktop computer.
How to power your Raspberry Pi?
To power a Raspberry Pi, you need to connect it to a power source.
The most common way is through a USB to microUSB or USB-C cable, depending on the model, connected to a USB power adapter. Make sure the adapter provides the appropriate voltage and current for your Raspberry Pi model.
Steps:

Identify the power connector: Older models, such as the Raspberry Pi 3 and earlier, use a microUSB port, while newer models, such as the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, use USB-C.
Connect the power adapter: Plug the USB power adapter into the wall outlet and then connect the corresponding USB cable to the Raspberry Pi’s port.
Verify the power: If everything is connected correctly, the Raspberry Pi should turn on. Some models have indicator lights that will help you confirm the power.

Keep in mind:

Voltage and current: The Raspberry Pi needs a 5V power source. The required current may vary depending on the model, but generally, between 2.5A and 3A is recommended for models like the Raspberry Pi 4. (Source: Bret).
Phone chargers: Although some phone chargers may work, it is recommended to use a power adapter designed specifically for the Raspberry Pi to ensure optimal performance and avoid power issues.
USB Hubs: If you need to connect multiple USB devices to the Raspberry Pi, consider using an externally powered USB hub to avoid power supply problems.
Batteries: If you need to power the Raspberry Pi with a battery, make sure to use a DC/DC converter to step up the battery voltage to 5V.
Raspberry Pi Pico: The Raspberry Pi Pico can be powered with an external battery connected via a microUSB to USB cable.

en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.title: Cable RG6
en/glossary/conc-rg6-cable.content:
An RG6 cable is a type of coaxial cable → used primarily for the transmission of cable television, satellite, and internet signals, as well as for some high-definition video applications.
It is known for its ability to handle higher frequencies and reduce signal loss, making it a popular choice for both indoor and outdoor installations.
Main features:

Center conductor: Generally, an RG6 cable has a copper center conductor, sometimes copper-clad steel.
Dielectric insulation: An insulating material that separates the center conductor from the shielding mesh.
Shielding: The RG6 cable features a shielding layer to protect the signal from electromagnetic interference (EMI) and noise. It can be single, double (foil and braid), or quad-shielded.
Impedance: Typically 75 ohms, which is the standard impedance for most video and television applications.
Applications: It is used to connect antennas, cable boxes, satellite dishes, and to carry internet and television signals.
Advantages: It offers better signal quality and lower signal loss than other coaxial cables like the RG59, especially in high-frequency and long-distance applications.

In summary, the RG6 cable is a versatile, high-performance coaxial cable, ideal for transmitting video and data signals across different media and distances.

en/glossary/conc-router.title: Router (Enrutador)
en/glossary/conc-router.content:
A Router is a device that connects different networks and decides which path data should travel to reach its destination.
In our technological kitchen:

The Router is The Distributor.
Its job is to take the dishes coming out of the kitchen and know exactly which table (cell phone or computer) they should go to without them getting cold or getting lost along the way.
If two people order sancocho at the same time, the distributor ensures that each one receives theirs correctly.


How does it help the community?
The router allows many neighbors to connect to the same Local Network → at the same time. As the “Distributor,” it manages traffic so that everyone has a smooth experience, distributing the Bandwidth → equitably.

Related concepts

Local Network →
WiFi Signal →
DHCP Protocol →


Change log




















DateChangeAuthor2026-04-05Analogy update (The Kitchen)David2025-06-05Initial versionSOLE

en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.title: Memoria SD
en/glossary/conc-sdmemory.content:
A MicroSD card is a very small portable storage device.
Sometimes they are simply called SD, although it is more accurate to name them according to their size: SD (the largest), MiniSD (the medium ones), and MicroSD (the smallest).
It is important to know the class of the memory, as this indicates the read and write speed. Generally, it is good to have class 10 memory cards to ensure good speed and to prevent the devices using them from having issues accessing the stored data.

en/glossary/conc-server.title: Servidor
en/glossary/conc-server.content:
A server is a type of computer or computer system designed to provide services, resources, or information to other devices or users through a network →.
It functions as an intermediary that processes requests and sends them to other computers or individual users. These services can include file storage, database management, website hosting, among others.
In essence, a server is a powerful computer designed to handle large amounts of data and perform complex tasks efficiently for multiple users simultaneously.
Some common examples of servers include:

Web servers: Store and serve web pages.
Mail servers: Manage the sending and receiving of email messages.
Database servers: Store and manage large sets of data.
File servers: Allow for the storage and shared access of files.
Application servers: Run applications for various users.

According to their purpose, we can classify them into:

Test servers: A test server, also known as a staging or pre-production server, is an independent environment used to test and validate applications or websites before their deployment on a production server (the one used by end users). The key difference lies in their purpose: the test server is used for exhaustive testing, while the production server is for actual use.
Production server: Its purpose is to serve applications and websites to end users, who interact with the application or website. It contains the actual user data and the running application. It is open to the public or a specific group of users.

Servers are a fundamental part of the internet infrastructure and corporate networks, as they allow for communication and the exchange of information between different devices and users.

en/glossary/conc-simcard.title: Tarjeta SIM
en/glossary/conc-simcard.content:
A SIM card, or Subscriber Identity Module, is a small, removable card that is inserted into mobile phones → and other devices to identify them on a cellular network and allow them to access services such as calls, messages, and data.
It functions as a digital key that allows your device to connect to your carrier’s network and authenticate you as a user.
What does a SIM card do?

Identification: The SIM stores unique information about you, such as your phone number and service plan details.
Authentication: It allows your device to securely connect to your carrier’s network.
Access to services: It enables making calls, sending messages, and using mobile data.
Storage: It can also save contacts, SMS messages, and other user data.

How have SIM cards evolved since their creation?

Original SIM: Had the size of a credit card.
MiniSIM: Smaller than the original.
MicroSIM: More compact than the MiniSIM, used in devices like the iPhone 4.
NanoSIM: The smallest, used in most modern smartphones.
eSIM: A SIM integrated directly into the device, allowing for carrier changes without the need to swap a physical card.

en/glossary/conc-smartphone.title: Teléfono móvil inteligente
en/glossary/conc-smartphone.content:
A mobile phone, also known as a cell phone, is a portable electronic device that allows making and receiving phone calls through a wireless connection, using a mobile communications network.
In addition to basic calling and messaging functions, modern mobile phones, especially smartphones, offer a wide range of features such as Internet access, applications, a camera, a media player, and more.

Mobile communication: The main function of a mobile phone is to allow long-distance voice communication through a wireless network.
Portability: The distinctive characteristic of mobile phones is their ability to be carried and used while on the move, within the mobile network’s coverage area.
Additional functionalities: Smartphones, in particular, integrate numerous additional features, such as internet access, web browsing, music and video playback, photo and video capture, and the execution of applications.
Mobile networks: Mobile phones connect to mobile communication networks →, which use base stations to transmit radio signals and enable communication between devices.
Evolution: Mobile phones have evolved from simple devices for calls to multifunctional smartphones, thanks to technological advances such as the miniaturization of components, the improvement of mobile networks, and the development of software and applications.

en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.title: Protocolo SSH
en/glossary/conc-ssh-protocol.content:
SSH (Secure Shell) is a protocol that allows you to access and manage a computer or server remotely through an encrypted and secure connection.
In our tech kitchen:

SSH is The Master Key.
It allows the kitchen manager to enter through the back door without having to be there physically.
Most importantly, this key travels inside a sealed envelope (encrypted); no one along the way can see what the manager is doing or steal their password.


What is it for?
In a Pocket Server →, we use SSH to install programs, organize folders, or fix problems from our own chair, using the Terminal →. It is the preferred tool for tinkerers to work remotely.

Related concepts

Terminal →
Server →
Firewall →

en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.title: Identificador SSID
en/glossary/conc-ssid-identifier.content:
The SSID, or Service Set Identifier, is the name that identifies a Wi-Fi network →.
It is the name you see when you search for available wireless networks on your device, such as a phone or computer. It allows users to distinguish between different Wi-Fi networks in a given area and connect to the desired network. (Source: Lenovo)
In simpler terms, the SSID is like the name of a Wi-Fi network, such as “John’s House” or “Starbucks_Wi-Fi.” Devices use the SSID to find and connect to the correct network. It is important to remember that the SSID does not provide security on its own; network security is achieved through protocols such as WPA2 or WPA3. (Source: Kaspersky)
In summary, the SSID is the name that identifies a Wi-Fi network and makes it easier for users to connect to the desired network. (Source: Fortinet)

en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.title: Almacenamiento (Disco Duro y SSD)
en/glossary/conc-storage-disk.content:
Storage is the part of the computer responsible for saving your files, photos, programs, and the operating system permanently.
If we continue with the kitchen analogy:

Storage is the pantry or a large warehouse outside the house.
You keep your bulk food (your files) there so they are preserved even when you stop cooking.
When you need something to cook, you take it out of the pantry and place it on the countertop (the RAM Memory →).


Types of storage
As technology advances, we have moved from slow but giant “pantries” to ultra-fast “refrigerators.”
HDD (Hard Disk Drive)
This is the traditional hard drive. It works with spinning platters and a needle that “reads” the information physically. It is like a very large and cheap warehouse, but slow. It remains the best option for storing massive amounts of files (such as in Servers →) because you can have a lot of space for little money.
SSD (Solid State Drive)
This is the solid-state drive. It has no moving parts; it uses chips (like USB flash drives). It is much faster than an HDD. Imagine that the pantry is now right next to the countertop and it is very easy to take things out. The computer turns on in seconds!
NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express)
This is the most recent evolution of SSDs. They are tiny and connect directly to the “brain” of the computer. It is like having an automatic system that puts the ingredients into the cook’s hand instantly.

The real world and technology
Technology was designed by imitating how we humans organize ourselves. Networks, for example, are like water pipes: information flows from one side to the other. Servers are like community warehouses where we all store something (the cloud). Understanding these concepts helps us see that the digital world is just a translation of what we already know how to do in the kitchen or the workshop.

Related concepts

RAM Memory →
Server →
SD Memory →

en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.title: Memoria SWAP
en/glossary/conc-swap-memory.content:
SWAP memory, also known as swap space or virtual memory, is a section of the hard drive → that an operating system → uses as if it were RAM memory → when physical RAM is running low.
It acts as an extension of RAM memory, allowing the system to move less-used data from RAM to the hard drive to free up space in RAM for more active processes. (Source: Aprendo Linux)
In simpler terms, swap memory is like a temporary storage space on the hard drive that the operating system uses when it needs more memory than it has physically available in RAM. When a program needs more memory, the operating system can move less-used data from RAM to swap to free up space in RAM and continue running programs.
Why is it used?

Prevent memory exhaustion: When RAM is full, the operating system can use swap to prevent applications from crashing or becoming unstable.
Allow running more programs: Swap memory allows running more programs simultaneously than would be possible with only the available RAM.
Hibernation: In some operating systems, swap memory is used to save the system state when hibernating.

How does it work?

RAM exhaustion: When RAM fills up, the operating system identifies the least-used data.
Transfer to swap: This less-used data is moved from RAM to the swap space on the hard drive.
RAM release: The freed RAM can be used for other processes that need memory.
Access to swap: When the data moved to swap needs to be accessed, the operating system reloads it into RAM, and sometimes moves other less-used data to swap.

Advantages and disadvantages:

Advantages: Allows running more programs and prevents memory issues when RAM is full.
Disadvantages: Accessing swap memory (on the hard drive) is much slower than accessing RAM, which can affect system performance if used excessively.

Swap memory is an important tool for memory management in computer systems, especially in those with limited amounts of RAM. Although useful, it is important to keep in mind that excessive use of swap can negatively affect system performance.

en/glossary/conc-system-folders.title: Carpetas y Rutas
en/glossary/conc-system-folders.content:
Folders (or directories) and Paths are the way the operating system organizes information so it doesn’t get lost.
In our technological kitchen:

It is the System of Shelves and Jars.
A Path is the exact address of where you stored something. For example: Cupboard > Top Shelf > Salt Jar.
On a computer, a path looks like this: /home/user/documents/photo.jpg.


How are they organized?
Each system has its own “organizing style”:

In Windows: Everything starts with a letter, usually the C: drive. (E.g.: C:\Users\David\Photos).
In Linux: There are no letters. Everything originates from a common root called / (slash). It is like a large tree where each branch is a folder. (Always think of it as a tree).
The server folder: By convention, things that the world can see on your server are usually stored in a folder called /var/www/. It’s like the kitchen counter!

en/glossary/conc-terminal.title: Terminal o consola
en/glossary/conc-terminal.content:
In computing, a terminal or console is a device used to connect to a computer; in more technical terms, it is a text-based user interface that allows interaction with an operating system → or an application.
Historically, it referred to a physical device with a keyboard and a monitor, but nowadays, it usually refers to a software application that emulates that function, that is, a program that allows us to communicate directly with our operating system without the need to use graphical interfaces.
In more detail:

Terminal: It is the interface that allows you to execute commands, control applications, and view results in a text environment. Currently, it more commonly refers to a program that emulates a physical terminal, allowing interaction with the operating system through commands.
Console: Traditionally, the console referred to a physical device, such as a keyboard and monitor, connected directly to the computer. Today, the term can also refer to the terminal interface used to manage and configure systems, and it is also used to refer to the management interface for cloud services.
Difference between console and terminal: Although the terms are often used interchangeably, the console can refer to the physical device, while the terminal can refer to the software that emulates that device. In practice, both terms are used to describe the command-line interface that users interact with to give instructions to the system.

In summary, both the terminal and the console are interfaces that allow communication with the operating system, whether through a physical device (historically) or a software program (currently).

References

Terminal on Wikipedia

en/glossary/conc-umts.title: UMTS (Sistema Universal de Telecomuniaciones Móviles
en/glossary/conc-umts.content:
UMTS (Universal Mobile Telecommunications System) is a third-generation (3G) mobile telephony technology that provides high-speed internet access and multimedia services, succeeding GSM (2G) →.
Its main purpose is to offer broadband wireless communications with higher download and upload speeds than previous networks, allowing for more efficient web browsing, video calls, and the use of multimedia applications.
(Source: 1NCE)
What is UMTS used for?

Mobile broadband internet access: Allows devices to connect to the Internet at significantly higher speeds than the previous generation (2G).
Multimedia services: Facilitates high-speed data transmission, enabling the use of bandwidth-intensive applications such as video calling, downloading multimedia content, and smooth web browsing.
Higher quality and capacity: Offers superior communication quality, similar to that of a fixed network, and allows more users to connect to the network simultaneously.
Evolution towards 4G/LTE: Although it is a 3G technology, successive improvements such as HSPA (High Speed Packet Access) and HSPA+ brought its capabilities closer to those of 4G (LTE) networks, extending the lifespan of the network infrastructure.
Compatibility with diverse devices: Supports a wider variety of terminals and applications, including “Internet of Things” (IoT) devices that require intensive data usage.

Key features of UMTS


CDMA technology: Uses W-CDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) technology to transmit data at high speeds across a wider radio frequency band.


Network components: Includes the Universal Terrestrial Radio Access Network (UTRAN), the Core Network (CN), and the User Equipment (UE).


Improvements over GSM:
Offers speeds of up to 2 Mbps (initially), with subsequent improvements through HSPA and HSPA+ reaching up to 42 Mbps or more, far exceeding the speeds of GSM networks.


Referencias | References

Emnify
