en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.title: Conexión USB
en/glossary/conc-usb-connection.content:
The USB (Universal Serial Bus) is the standard that allows almost any electronic device to communicate with another. It is like a smart plug that not only carries power, but also information (photos, music, documents).
Following our kitchen analogy:

The USB port is like a wall outlet, but one that works for the blender, the radio, and even for charging your cell phone.
Before, every appliance brand had its own strange plug; USB arrived so that everyone would use the same one.


The history of standards
At the beginning, USB was a mess: there was USB-A (the large rectangular one), micro-USB (the one for old cell phones), and mini-USB. Each one had a different shape and you never had the cable you needed.
Brands wanted you to buy their specific cables, which generated tons of electronic waste (cables that are no longer useful for anything).

The power of the people and USB-C
USB-C is the small, rounded connector that can be plugged in either way (it has no “right side up” or “upside down”). What makes it special is not just its technology, but how it became the standard:

Citizen movements: Groups of people, consumer organizations, and movements like the “Right to Repair” pressured governments.
Laws for the planet: In places like the European Union, laws were created to force all brands (including the most stubborn ones) to use a single universal charger: USB-C.
Result: Thanks to people coming together to demand less waste and more convenience, today we can use a single cable for the computer, the cell phone, and the headphones. A great triumph of the collective over the market!


What is it used for?

Transferring energy: Charging your devices.
Transferring data: Moving files between a USB Flash Drive → and the computer.
Connecting tools: Keyboards, mice, cameras, and even fans.


Related concepts

USB Flash Drive →
Storage (Hard Drive and SSD) →
Hardware →

en/glossary/conc-username.title: Nombre de usuario
en/glossary/conc-username.content:
A username is a unique string of characters that identifies a user in a computer system, such as a social network, a website, or an application.
It is used to log in and access your account, and is generally used in conjunction with a password to verify your identity. (Source: Dashlane)
In detail, a username:

Uniquely identifies the user: It allows each user to be distinguished within the system, avoiding conflicts and ensuring that the correct permissions are granted.
Is used to log in: It is how you identify yourself to access your account and the resources associated with it.
Can be public or private: In some systems, the username is visible to other users, while in others it may be private.
Must be unique within the system: There cannot be two users with the same username to avoid confusion.
Can be alphanumeric: It generally consists of a combination of letters and numbers, although some systems allow special characters such as underscores or dots.
Is different from a password: The password is an authentication factor that protects access to your account, while the username is simply an identifier.

en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.title: WhatsApp
en/glossary/conc-whatsapp.content:
WhatsApp is an instant messaging and calling application, owned by Meta, that allows users to send messages, make voice and video calls, and share files over the internet.
It is widely used for both personal communication and business.
It allows you to send text, voice, and video messages, make voice and video calls, and share files such as photos, documents, locations, and contacts.
Although it is primarily known for personal use to communicate with friends and family, it has a business version called WhatsApp Business, which allows you to interact with customers, manage sales, and provide customer support.
Be careful! WhatsApp is usually included in the data plans of most mobile operators in Colombia, although it may incur additional charges for data and downloads not specified in your plan.
It is available for different operating systems →, including Android and iOS, and also has a web version.
The application ensures that personal conversations, calls, and multimedia content are protected with end-to-end encryption, which means that only the sender and the receiver can access them.
The WhatsApp interface is simple and intuitive, facilitating communication between users, especially with those who are already part of your contact list.

en/glossary/conc-wifi.title: Señal WiFi
en/glossary/conc-wifi.content:
WiFi (or Wireless Fidelity) is a technology that allows devices to connect to a network without the need for cables, using radio waves.
In our technological kitchen:

WiFi is The Aroma of the Kitchen.
When the server → has the information ready, it “spreads” it through the air like the smell of a good stew.
Your cell phone or computer is like the “nose” that detects that aroma and connects to receive the information.
If you move too far away or there are very thick walls, the aroma (the signal) weakens until it disappears.


How to improve the aroma?
For WiFi to reach further in your community, it is important to place the Router → in a high place without obstacles, just as you would place a steaming pot near a window so that the smell invites everyone in.

en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.title: Antena tipo Yagi
en/glossary/conc-yagi-antenna.content:
A Yagi antenna → is a type of directional antenna, known for its high gain and ability to focus the signal in a specific direction.
It consists of a main element called the boom (or active element) and several shorter elements, called directors and reflectors, arranged along the boom.
How does it work?

Active element: This is the one connected directly to the transmitter or receiver and is where the main signal is generated or received.
Directors: These are elements shorter than the active element and are located in front of it, in the direction of the desired signal. They help focus the signal in that direction, increasing the antenna’s gain.
Reflector: This is an element longer than the active element and is located behind it. It reflects radio waves, helping to concentrate the signal in the desired direction and reduce the signal in the opposite direction, which increases the antenna’s directivity.

Main characteristics:

Directivity: Yagi antennas are highly directional, meaning they are more effective at transmitting or receiving signals in a specific direction.
Gain: Gain refers to the antenna’s ability to concentrate the signal in one direction. Yagi antennas have high gain, which allows them to transmit and receive signals over long distances.
Size: The size of a Yagi antenna can vary depending on the frequency it is designed for, but they are generally more compact than other directional antennas like parabolic ones.

Applications:

TV and radio reception: They are commonly used to improve television and radio signal reception, especially in areas with poor coverage.
Wireless communications: They are effective in point-to-point and point-to-multipoint links, where directional communication is required.
Amateur radio: Radio amateurs use Yagi antennas to communicate over long distances and participate in radio contests.
Radar systems: In some military and radar applications, Yagi antennas are used to focus and direct radar signals.

In summary, the Yagi antenna is a valuable tool for improving signal reception and transmission in various applications due to its high directivity and gain.

en/inspire/insp-big-questions.title: Todo comienza con una Gran Pregunta
en/inspire/insp-big-questions.content:
Download this solution to use it offline
This is an experience designed to spark curiosity in anyone in the world, leading them to use the Internet in groups to learn.
If you like it, you can download SOLE Voltaje Offline and take it to places that have little or no connectivity. Enjoy!
So, how can I know something I don’t know?
We are going to tell you a little story about how we learn.
[Taken from SOLE Colombia (2019) A conversation with Sugata Mitra]

  
  

Taken from SOLE Colombia (2019) A conversation with Sugata Mitra


Read the transcript
Historically, if you wanted to know something, the traditional way was to find someone who knew it and ask them. That is not very practical because you cannot always find the person in question or you cannot go see them, so it used to take a long time to learn things. All of this changed thanks to writing. People could write down what they knew, and if you wanted to know it, you would find it and read it.
But some people opposed writing. Surprisingly, the most famous of those who opposed writing was Socrates, the Greek philosopher. His objection was that you can read what someone has written, but you cannot ask them questions, and sometimes it is not easy to find what has been written either. That problem was solved with libraries, where the writings of many people are kept in the same place, but even that had a problem because, first of all, you have to find the library and go to it. Secondly, if you are reading something and you have a question, you have no one to ask.
This started to change thanks to the Internet. Now, you can find what anyone writes at any time, and while you are reading, if you have a question, you can (usually) find someone to ask. So, the two problems Socrates had, namely: 1) where do I find the writings and 2) who do I ask if I have a doubt, seem to have been solved thanks to the Internet.
To this, we must add one last thing: if reading is done with many people together, each one can ask the other. Therefore, a group of learners can build a very inexpensive place with little material available where they have a computer, the Internet, and can ask each other questions. In other words, it turns out to be very easy to create a learning environment by yourself, and that is what we call a Self-Organized Learning Environment or SOLE.
The idea is very simple and powerful: it is possible for learners to create their own learning environment using the Internet!


So, if you wanted to know the answer to something you don’t know, how would you do it?
Think of any person, like you, young or old, anywhere in the world who wants to answer a question they have always had and have never been able to solve: their possibilities for learning, from the oldest to the most recent, could be:
1. Ask someone who knows: Oral tradition
Look for someone around you who knows the answer to your Big Question. It could be a friend, your parents or grandparents, a teacher, or a neighbor.
If they don’t have the answer, ask them who might have it and travel together with this question to ask that other person.
This is how most ancestral knowledge is passed down, even today.
2. Search in writings: Textual transmission
Where are there writings on the subject of that question? At home, at a neighbor’s house, at school, at the public library, or somewhere in the nearest town?
Go and look for them together. As in the story of the libraries, knowledge can be passed on in writing, and librarians or teachers may know which books your answer might be in.
Imagine… This is how we have learned since writing was invented, and it has gradually become more equitable as public education becomes universal. However, there are many people who still do not have access to it.
Did you find the answer?


Yes!
Great! And did any new questions arise? Go back to asking someone who knows, or go back to searching in writings that you have within reach.


No.
Then where else can we find it? I suppose if you are reading this, it might sound obvious that you can search on the Internet. Just keep in mind that, in 2024, half of the people in the world DO NOT have access to the Internet.


3. Search on the Internet: Digital interconnection
Doing a search on the Internet is like having the largest library in the world in your pocket. Google or any other search engine, where you type your Big Question, is like the librarian who searches through all the texts, videos, audios, and other content on the Internet and offers them to you so you can explore them.
However, I don’t know if you know, but searching the Internet on your own is difficult. There are many answers to your Big Question; some are better than others, but there are also many wrong ones. There are even lies written by people or even machines, such as those called Artificial Intelligence (AI). Learning to judge that sea of information in order to learn is an art. The same thing happens when you ask someone who knows or search in writings.
The best way to overcome this is to doubt, be curious, and ask new questions. This is what scientists and artists do; they don’t settle for the first thing they learn. Although sometimes learning alone - being self-taught - is demanding, regardless of whether you have access to all the information.
4. Search on the Internet in a group: SOLEing
At SOLE Colombia, we have discovered that many people who do not have access to good education can learn to learn almost anything using the Internet in a group because they can doubt, be curious, and ask new questions together. It is like being self-taught but in a group, which is not only easier, more fun, and more powerful than using the Internet alone, but it also proposes a new way of being together. We call this SOLEing.

WHAT IS SOLE?
SOLE (Self-Organized Learning Environments) is a disruptive learning methodology that empowers communities to develop autonomy, collaboration, deep learning, and, most importantly, to solve real-life problems!
A SOLE session is simple. You need a space with people, a few computers with Internet access, and Big Questions. In a SOLE session, learners self-organize to find answers to questions using the Internet, without the need for a teacher.
WHAT IS THE GRANNY CLOUD?
Along with SOLE is the concept of the Granny. Research has shown that limited intervention from an untrained facilitator can promote thriving learning processes. The role of a Granny consists of sparking curiosity, asking questions, listening carefully, and providing a warm environment. The Granny Cloud is a network of volunteers from all professions and social backgrounds who connect remotely with SOLEs to co-facilitate and offer participants the opportunity to experience worlds far removed from their own.
And what if you don’t have the Internet?
If you don’t have the Internet, you will always be able to know more using the first options, even if they have the difficulties that Sugata Mitra mentions in the video.
However, at SOLE Colombia
At SOLE Voltaje, we have the idea that using the Internet in a group to learn is a way to have new, healthy human relationships that will allow us not only to change the way we learn and dialogue but also the way we create the world we want together. Furthermore, it will change the shape of the Internet to be more inclusive, diverse, and equitable. But for this, it is important that everyone can access the Internet.

en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.title: How to build memory in a SOLE Lab?
en/inspire/insp-build-memory-solelab.content:
Purpose: to agilely collect the history of the Boca de Camarones SOLE Lab from the perspective of each group of collaborators (Boca de Camarones Community, SOLE Colombia, and Internet Society Foundation)
Instructions
In groups, tell the life story of the SOLE Lab. On colored panels, draw:

1st panel: the beginning—why did the idea or need arise?
Last panel: What is the SOLE Lab today and how does it feel to have it?
Intermediate panels: milestones or relevant moments in the history of the SOLE Lab.



How do our SOLE Lab stories connect? On a canvas, we will organize the drawings, connecting the stories with yarn.


How does my life story connect with the history of the SOLE Lab?


Development of the device

The experiences narrated below are the result of what each group said about their experiences in relation to the SOLE LAB. To avoid misrepresentation, we use ““ as a way to quote what the person actually said. In other parts of the text, the people are paraphrased, striving to maintain fidelity to what was expressed throughout the session.
We use the word milestone to refer to those events or occurrences that are significant to the person telling the story.

Boca de Camarones Community
Elainer:
Milestone 1: “The SOLE LAB originated from when I worked at the Puntos Vive Digital.” Elainer was an ICT manager. Once this project ended for him, the idea of having a SOLE LAB emerged.
Milestone 2: He remembers having done a SOLE about what internet connection is.
Milestone 3: When he heard the story of the SOLE LAB, he realized it could be the starting point for sharing with the community. An event he remembers with joy is the SOLE Festival.
Milestone 4: “For my work, I had to do a webinar. I remembered what I learned in SOLE and I was able to do it. The grandmother allowed me to lose my fear of screens.”
Milestone 5: Elainer mentions that SOLE has not been the only thing done in that space. The SOLE LAB has been used as a point of interest for tourists. Tourists rest and connect to the internet; furthermore, they are told the history of that space.
Caril:
Milestone 6: Caril tells us everything she learned about shrimp thanks to a SOLE. “Thanks to a great question, we learned about shrimp: what does a shrimp eat?”
Marcelo and Ana María:
Milestone 7: Both organized a SOLE with the children. They say it was very exciting for the community.

Marcelo works with the children of the community and has ideas that can generate economic sustainability, with video games or by offering the connection space to foreigners.
Marcelo remembers when the materials for the construction of the SOLE LAB started to arrive and everything that this process entailed. For his part, he remembers how rewarding it was to support the construction and see it finished.
Ana María takes care of the space, the garden, and the SOLE LAB. Ana María mentions that they have managed and held bingos and other activities of interest to the community.

Internet Society Foundation
Gustavo
Milestone 1: “Everyone should have access to the internet.” For this reason, ISOC grants exist, in which they are interested in the internet being used in a communal and open way. For this reason, the SOLE LAB is a space of great interest to him and to the mission of his work.
Milestone 2: For Gustavo, the SOLE LAB is a way to connect the internet and people.
Milestone 3: For him, the SOLE LAB should have a flag showing that it is a space to democratize knowledge.
Milestone 4: “We think differently, but our stories connect.”
SOLE COLOMBIA
Milestone 1 [2015]: Sanjay wondered what a library of the future with the internet, mediated by the SOLE methodology, would be like.
Milestone 2 [2017]: They met Elainer and learned about the Puntos Vive Digital, where he worked.
Milestone 3 [2018]: The first version of the SOLE LAB was made in La Sevillana.
Milestone 4 [2021]: The first SOLE LAB was funded through the Internet Society call for proposals.
Milestone 5 [2022]: Sanjay and Belén travel to Boca de Camarones and begin to manage the design and construction of the first SOLE LAB.
Milestone 6 [2023]: “Now the first SOLE LAB in Boca de Camarones is a reality. It exists and works, and we want it to be sustainable for the community.”
Findings and learnings

All the stories of the SOLE LAB connect people, stories, and affections. It is interesting how the tastes and passions of the people in the community and in SOLE are empowered.
Carrying out a SOLE LAB implies the synergy and meeting of several common wills.
The stories exceed the SOLE LAB; in other words, this space becomes a pretext to live and coexist in other ways.
Having been part of the project generates pride and dignity.

Did you know you can use the game to create community agreements? 💭
In the Fish Game, we learn through a simple but powerful experience: the more we fish for ourselves, the fewer fish remain for others. But when we work together, we ensure there is enough for everyone.
This game is a metaphor for real life. The fish are not just fish. 🌱 They represent the resources we share: the internet, land, food, even the air we breathe!
Think of it this way: imagine sharing an internet plan with your neighbors. If we all use it consciously, we can make it go further and benefit the entire community. But if we only think about our own interests, the resource is quickly depleted, harming everyone. Are you ready to make agreements with your community?

en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.title: How to change the world from your home? Meet the Grandmothers' Cloud
en/inspire/insp-granny-cloud.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
What is The Granny Cloud?
The Granny Cloud is a concept born alongside the SOLE idea that captures the spirit of those who support learning from a loving perspective, those who encourage us to learn in a subtle way, offering warm encouragement, asking pertinent questions, and marveling at our discoveries.
They are people who have fun learning, are curious, and enjoy interacting with learners. Sugata Mitra called this perspective “the Granny’s gaze.” Suneeta Kulkarni, his research partner, formed The Granny Cloud, and at SOLE Colombia, we take up their mantle and legacy to form La Nube de Abuelitas (The Granny Cloud) in Spanish.
Who makes it up?
We are volunteers, men and women, from all around the world. We have Grannies in Spain, Portugal, Denmark, Mexico, Colombia, the United States, Peru, Chile, Vietnam… there are Grannies everywhere!
There is a Granny Cloud Coordinator, who is in charge of managing the sessions, calling for and communicating the schedules, and the people who will be attending each session that requests a Granny.
Every year, coinciding with the start of the projects, new Grannies join who discover their motivation and whom we train in the methodology so they can SOLE and enjoy this very rewarding role.
How can you be a Granny?
What you need to be a Granny is the desire to connect with communities that learn through the SOLE Methodology. Do you want tools? You can download the Granny Manual and find stories about Grannies on the SOLE Colombia website. You can also request to join The Granny Cloud through this form, and we will get in touch with you to tell you everything.
Stay tuned to our social media and other platforms (take a look at our website) to know when the next “costurero” (sewing circle/gathering) is called and what the schedules for the next SOLEs are—don’t miss them!

en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.title: La Nube de Abuelitas: qué pasa cuando no hay conexión
en/inspire/insp-granny-no-connection.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
There is a question I get asked a lot when I talk about what a Granny does in a SOLE: what happens if there is no connection? The answer is easy to tell, but not easy to understand. I always say: you figure it out! And people look at me wondering, “but if it’s a video call and there is no connection, what is the point of being a SOLE Granny?”
What really happens is that you realize that communication and presence don’t need many frills to happen.
Obviously, if the SOLE has a super good connection, everything is very organic. People chat, we all hear each other, we can interact easily, we converse and do incredible searches… it feels easy, pleasant, and, when finished, the heart feels full and happy.
When those conditions are not met and the connection is difficult, the image is pixelated, the sound is choppy, we don’t even hear the Big Question, or even the video call chat doesn’t seem to work synchronously. Frustration invades us, we don’t understand what is happening, we want to hang up and continue with our commitments, because this makes no sense… This feeling is multiplied if it is one of our first connections, if we have just started in La Nube de Abuelitas.
At the same time, on the other side, there is a community that also doesn’t hear us, sees us blurry, there are many of them, the computer screen where the Granny is is small, the sound coming out of the speaker is very low. Maybe it’s hot or it’s after lunch. In the Tuning Visits, for example, it is the first time that communities do a SOLE and they don’t quite understand what is happening, how they are going to find answers on the Internet, how the computer is handled, what they have to do at each moment, or who is that person trying to talk to them from who knows where.
From experience, I tell you: the power of the Internet is like the power of water… it seeps through anywhere! It seeps through everywhere! And it is when a message, somehow, from the other side of the world tells you “I am with you, that question you are asking is great, I am searching and I found (…) congratulations on that research, I look forward to seeing you for the next SOLE!” and that is when the environment fills with joy and lets us all know that we came here to learn, that we are TOGETHER. And that TOGETHER takes on a much larger and more powerful meaning.
From here we thank all those who did not give up, those who sent a question or an answer via WhatsApp, those who voted in deferred time, all those who also followed the game, minute by minute… THANK YOU to all!

en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.title: Preguntas y respuestas sobre la experiencia de ser una Abuelita
en/inspire/insp-granny-questions.content:
Download this Inspiration to use offline
What is the minimum amount of time I must commit to the sessions?
The key to learning is consistency. We are aware that life and responsibilities change, and that is why some Grandmas will not be able to continue for an indefinite period. If you cannot commit continuously, or for a long time, just tell us what you can do: it could be an occasional session or interacting with the coordination team, or other Grandmas, to support us with ideas on how to better face the challenges that may come.
How does seeing the differences in “privilege” between your environment and theirs affect us?
Feel confident in sharing your reality and your world with others: we enrich ourselves, get inspired, and explore possibilities when we come into contact with the realities of others.
This experience touches us all equally. You also discover and learn from other worlds. You also enrich yourself with this experience. Let this experience and these people enter your life!
What happens to the children or adults when the experience with the Grandma ends?
It is a question that many have asked and that generates concern. Although some experiences are shorter than expected, the impact it generates on children and people in general remains present. Read our SOLE stories to know what they say about The Grandma Cloud in the territories where we have accompanied SOLE sessions to let yourself be touched by the magic.
What should I do if I am contacted by the media to talk about/film my interaction as part of The Grandma Cloud?
If we are interacting with children, we must look after the children’s interests and not expose them unduly. Before speaking to the media or taking photos or videos of the people, contact the SOLE Colombia team.
How is The Grandma Cloud funded?
As we have mentioned, the Grandmas are volunteers and, thanks to this, many children, young people, and adults have been able to connect and share experiences. We want it to continue to be this way, although, perhaps, at some point we can explore new ways to maintain the relationship with the Grandmas.
And if I cannot be a Grandma, can I help in any other way?
There are always opportunities to join this global movement to transform the future of learning. At SOLE Colombia, we are open to exploring the best way to involve you. You can explore the roles of the SOLE Colombia Community and find where you feel most comfortable. Tell us what interests you or if you have any proposals!
If you still have unresolved questions, write to us at hola@solecolombia.org, we are just a message away.

en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.title: Have you ever wondered how the internet, electricity, or cell signal reaches you?
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-travels.content:
Every day we check messages on our cell phones, turn on a light, or receive a phone call.
Everything seems very mundane, but 150 years ago it was magic when cities like Bogotá - in Colombia - saw the miracle of electric light for the first time.
[This is how light came to Bogotá](www.senalmemoria.co/piezas/luz-llego-bogota#:~:text=Bogotá fue la primera ciudad,inconvenientes de ahí en adelante)

en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.title: How does the Internet work?
en/inspire/insp-how-internet-works.content:
Download this Inspiration to use it offline
Think about when you go to a restaurant and order a cup of coffee. You, as the client, ask or consult the waiter, and they go to the kitchen, return a while later, and serve you the cup of coffee, ready, like a good server. You aren’t quite sure how they prepared it, but you know it’s a cup of coffee when you taste it. The Internet works in a similar way. Let’s see.

  
  SOLE Colombia, 2024.

When you connect to the internet and have a question, what you do is consult it from a cell phone or computer, and you are communicating with many computers belonging to other people or companies that store what you want to find.
The information you want to consult can be a webpage, a video, a photo, a video call, a file, or a message. These are some of the formats of digital files that are sent over the internet.
The cell phone, computer, or tablet from which you connect to the internet is called the client.
The computer where the information you are consulting is stored is called the server.
How does information travel across the Internet?
For the information sent by a server to reach your home, neighborhood, rural area, or community, the client you use connects to the Internet. Let’s take, for example, your cell phone somewhere in Colombia and the fact that the answer is found on a server in Europe. This is the great adventure your question takes.

  
  How does your question travel across the Internet? SOLE Colombia, 2024.

Your cell phone connects via electromagnetic or wireless waves to one or several cell phone towers. Your question travels in the form of zeros “0” and ones “1” to one of those towers and goes down through a cable that goes underground and leads to some central cable hub. Then, it is redirected to a maritime port where that cable connects to a submarine cable. This goes under the ocean to the other continent and then comes out of the water to other cable points that take your question to the place where the server containing your answer is located. The server receives your question and responds with the information it has stored—also in zeros “0” and ones “1”—and it is sent back along that same route to your phone. And all of that happens in a matter of milliseconds! It’s incredible, don’t you think?
Diver installing a submarine cable

  
  Taken from Erbauer 2. Klasse Christopher Farmer, from Taylorsville.

Internal structure of a submarine cable

  
  Taken from: youtu.be/k1SMnnddpvI

Global map of submarine Internet cables

  
  Global map of submarine Internet cables. Data by Greg Mahlknecht, map by OpenStreetMap contributors (CC BY-SA 2.0).

It must be kept in mind that submarine cables allow us to transmit data so that telecommunications services can exist. The reason why information travels so fast is that the cables are made of fiber optics, that is, glass. This means that the information, the zeros “0” and “1”, are sent in the form of light, and light is what travels faster than anything else in the universe.
Isn’t it tremendous what we humans have invented?

en/inspire/insp-internet-in-group.title: When was the last time you used the internet with a group?
en/inspire/insp-internet-in-group.content:
Download this Inspiration to use it offline
So, let’s go back to the beginning: when was the last time you used the Internet in a group? Perhaps that memory—sharing a search, a screen, a question—is the beginning of another possible Internet. The Future Library is just that: proof that other Internets are possible, and that we are already creating them.

Reload Your SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca.
That is what we are creating with The Future Library: an ecosystem where access is not the end, but the starting point. A space where the network does not just connect devices, but also stories, doubts, and intuitions; a space to connect and ask questions without fear.
In the SOLE Labs we have seen how, when a community gathers around a screen, something changes. Girls, young people, and elders asking questions together. The Internet stops being a flow of information that we consume alone and becomes a shared territory. In a group, questions arise that do not appear when we are alone. Memories mix, curiosity awakens, collective projects are born. Using the Internet in a group is, in itself, a radical act because it challenges speed, noise, and the instruction to accept without questioning.

Plug in your SOLE Lab in Dominguillo, Cauca.
The Internet has become a personal space of consumption; “being connected” does not really mean being connected to others or connecting with others. And that is what changes when we use the Internet in a group.

SOLE Festival in Boca de Camarones, La Guajira.
Today, almost three billion people in the world remain disconnected. And that digital exclusion cuts across bodies, languages, and landscapes. It is not just a technical problem: it is a silent way of saying who counts and who doesn’t. But that is not all; those of us who have access to the Internet usually use it, not to connect, but to isolate ourselves further from those around us. We use it to order food, to find out about others’ lives, to buy things, to read about what interests us. We rarely use it to cook with others, to meet with others, to exchange knowledge, to create together.
Maybe you don’t remember. Because most of the time we connect alone: in front of a cell phone, a laptop, or a tablet. The Internet experience has become intimate, individual, and often passive. We accept answers that appear without asking, we navigate through algorithms that predict what we want before we say it. But there is something lost when we use the Internet in solitude: the possibility of looking each other in the eye while we search, of asking ourselves out loud, of inventing together.
When was the last time you used the Internet in a group?
While millions remain without Internet, those of us who have access use it each on our own. What if the future of the Internet was to use it in a group?

en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.title: How does a message travel from your mobile phone to your friends' phones?
en/inspire/insp-internet-signal-transmis.content:
Download this Inspiration to use it offline
The Internet signal is transmitted through physical infrastructure such as fiber optic and copper cables, as well as radio waves (Wi-Fi) and, to a lesser extent, via satellite or mobile networks (4G/5G). Data is converted into electrical or light pulses (bits) that travel through these media to their destination, using routers and other equipment to send and receive information.
Guided Media (wired):

Fiber optic: Transmits data as light pulses through thin glass strands.
Copper (Coaxial cable and twisted pair): Uses metal wires to carry electrical signals, such as in ADSL connections.
Submarine cables: Most global Internet traffic travels through fiber optic cables laid under the ocean.

Wireless Media (without cables):

Wi-Fi: Uses radio waves to connect devices (such as your phone or computer) to a router.
Mobile networks (3G, 4G, 5G): Signals are transmitted through antennas and cell towers to provide Internet access on mobile devices.
Satellite: Sends and receives signals to and from a satellite in orbit.

How does the process work?

Conversion to bits: When you send data (such as an email), your computer converts it into pulses of electricity or light (bits).
Transmission: These bits travel through physical infrastructure (cables, air, or space) to network equipment.
Routing: Routers and other network equipment direct these bits along the most efficient path to their destination.
Reception: On the receiving device, the bits are converted back into the original information that you can see or use.

(Source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medio_de_transmisi%C3%B3n)

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.title: How did internet improve in Cáceres, Antioquia?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-caceres.content:
In the community of Altos del Tigre, in the municipality of Cáceres, five community leaders are turning something almost impossible into a reality: improving Internet access in their community.
Yadiris Vaquero, Luz Cenith Acevedo, Kenia Yepes, Blanca Ofir Moreno, and David Ojeda, SOLE Ambassadors for their community, have been working for some time to ensure that having Internet stops being a hidden treasure in their territory. Because yes, in Cáceres, as in many places around Colombia, a connection has always been a luxury.
This year, however, something changed. Starting with the Tuning Visit back in May, the Ambassadors and other members of the community took the opportunity to learn together how the Internet works and why, precisely in Cáceres, having a signal was such a challenge. The answer? Basically, because there are no antennas for kilometers around and the telecommunications infrastructure is minimal.
But this did not discourage them. On the contrary, they got to work. They evaluated the situation, looked for solutions, and, with the support of the program, managed to find the ideal option for them: a Jangala device. This small but powerful device makes it possible to connect communities in hard-to-reach areas, and for the inhabitants of Cáceres, it was like a door to a new world.

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
Thus, thanks to the Jangala and the effort of the SOLE Ambassadors, and all the people in the community who joined together to manage to install this solution, Cáceres now has Internet at a community access point.

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
And for many, this achievement means much more than “having a connection”: it is an opportunity to learn, to be informed, and to stay up to date. Children, young people, and adults can now access information, participate in SOLE sessions, and, as they say, “solve those big questions that once seemed like something from another world.”
Listen to what one of the local handymen, who was encouraged to set up the Jangala antenna with the whole SOLE crew, has to say:

  
  

Arnulfo, Tuning Visits in Altos del Tigre, Antioquia, (2024).
The work of Yadiris, Luz Cenith, Kenia, Blanca Ofir, and David Ojeda has marked a turning point in Cáceres. Today, thanks to their dedication and the Jangala, the community not only has Internet, but is transforming how it uses it, discovering, sharing, and creating many possibilities for their community.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.title: How did internet improve in Chalán, Montes de María?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-chalan.content:
Chalán is a municipality in the department of Sucre, Colombia. In this region, rural communities (veredas) such as Monte Bello, Rancho Rojo, and Alemania are using the Internet in a unique way: they connect in groups to answer big questions, do homework, watch movies, or simply share their stories with the world.
Since 2023, Yulieth Farasica has been a SOLE Ambassador who has driven a major change in her community, leading collaborative learning sessions. Furthermore, this year she helped us install, teach, and promote the shared use of the Internet in her village, Alemania. Now, neighboring villages can also connect to the network, improving communication and access to information.
Listen to Yulieth as she tells her story about the lessons learned from connecting the community:

  
  

This is how Alemania is now a meeting point for Monte Bello, Rancho Rojo, and other nearby communities. People now travel to use this connection, which has been installed and put into operation through everyone’s effort.

  
  

There are now six ambassadors trained in the SOLE methodology who have learned how the Internet works and how to use their Jangala to share it with others!
Yulieth, Astrid, Yuranis, Johana, Celia, Maryuris, and Yolanda are changing the world. Thanks to their work, today in Chalán more children, youth, adults, and the elderly have access to the Internet. From neighboring villages like Monte Bello and Rancho Rojo, people arrive in Vda. Alemania to connect and be part of this network, which they themselves have created and sustained.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.title: How did internet improve in Colosó, Montes de María?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-coloso.content:
La Estación and the La Esmeralda Indigenous Council are just 15 minutes apart by motorcycle. Both are neighboring communities in the Colombian municipality of Colosó, in the department of Sucre. Until recently, neither of these communities had a public space to access the Internet as a group. However, since 2023, they have ventured into using the connectivity solutions we installed together in their territory to boost Self-Organized Learning.
No one is better than Mónica Vega, one of the star Ambassadors of La Estación, to share the story of how these communities are transforming their access to information, connection, and education. Are you ready to hear her? Don’t forget to turn up the volume!

  
  

Mónica Vega, during Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Did you hear her? It is incredible how their community has used Jangala and the Internet connection to strengthen the bonds between its members. But Mónica’s story doesn’t end there. This year, she decided to visit her neighboring community, La Esmeralda, to motivate more people to tinker with technology.
Even though Jangala was not the right solution for this community, Mónica and Gabriel, being the excellent “tinkerers” they are, got to work and nothing stopped them. Together we explored other connectivity options, and finally, with Mónica’s help, we installed an omnidirectional antenna and a router. Now, the Ambassadors of La Esmeralda are empowering their neighbors to use the Internet as a group.

  
  

Gabriel, during Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
In addition, the community has created its own website to tell the whole world about their products, traditions, services, territory, history, and customs. Community Internet is now in their hands!

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.title: How did internet improve in Dominguillo, Cauca?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-domingui.content:
In 2023, the community of Dominguillo began to experience an unexpected transformation, thanks to a new opportunity for connection. It all started when, through USAID’s Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program, implemented by the IOM, a device called Jangala arrived at the community’s public school library. This equipment allowed, for the first time, access to stable Internet, which quickly became an invaluable resource for everyone.
Here, presenting the Jangala or “Jang,” as they decided to call it, is Luis Miguel Mina—or Lucho, as we all know him—one of the SOLE Ambassadors we trained in 2023:

Franki, Lucho, and Mateo at the Inspiration Workshops in Dominguillo, Cauca (2023).
Inspiration Workshops, Dominguillo, Cauca (2023).
The device was installed in the library with the goal of facilitating SOLE (Self Organized Learning Environments) sessions, a methodology that invites participants to learn autonomously and collaboratively through Big Questions. With these tools in operation, the members of Dominguillo not only explored topics of interest to them, but also began to resolve questions about their culture and traditions, uniting the community around shared knowledge and rediscovering their roots through the Internet.
Listen to Luis Miguel Mina and Nancy Campo talk about this experience:

  
  

Luis Miguel Mina and Nancy Campo
SOLE Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals in Dominguillo, Santander de Quilichao (2023).
However, as time passed, the community could no longer continue using the school library for their SOLE sessions. By then, the impact of this connection had been so profound that the inhabitants of Dominguillo did not want to give it up. Convinced of the importance of having a community space for learning and connectivity, they sought support to create their own connection center: the Dominguillo SOLE Lab.
And… guess what? Together, we worked on the development of the SOLE Lab, a public space where chairs, tables, and computers were installed and Internet access was restored. With the SOLE Lab, the inhabitants of Dominguillo regained the opportunity to connect to the world, continue their SOLE sessions, and explore new ways of learning.

Dominguillo SOLE Lab, Cauca (2024).

Learning and community work at the SOLE Lab, Dominguillo (2024).

Children and youth participating in SOLE sessions, Dominguillo (2024).

Connectivity and global communication from Dominguillo, Cauca (2024).
Thanks to this effort, Dominguillo not only improved its Internet connection but also strengthened the community’s bond. Now, the SOLE Lab is a meeting point where the inhabitants continue to learn and share their knowledge.

  
  

Video of the “Enchufa Tu SOLE Lab” (Plug In Your SOLE Lab) in Dominguillo, Cauca, (2024).

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.title: How did internet improve in San Juan Nepomuceno, Montes de María?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nepomuce.content:
The following fragments are a compilation of testimonies, images, and scenes on how the use of group Internet in the municipality of San Juan Nepomuceno is transforming network access for neighboring communities, such as San José del Peñón and La Haya.
First Stop




SOLE Festivals, Montes de María, (2024).
To get to San José del Peñón, you have to cross seven rivers, cross your fingers that the rain doesn’t play a trick on you, and marvel at the majestic beauty of this territory. It is no coincidence that, upon arrival, a large sign proudly welcomes you: “San José del Peñón, magical, fertile, and powerful land.”
The geography of San José del Peñón, with its mountains and dense vegetation, prevents signals from nearby antennas from reaching the village. Installing a community connectivity solution was a challenge that required the effort of the entire community. With collective support and work, we managed to install, against all odds, our Rural KIT: a Yagi antenna and a router that now make it possible for the community to meet periodically to do SOLE.

  
  

Gabriel, Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).

  
  

Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Rafael Antonio García, a natural tinkerer in his community, tells us in his own words what the process was like to install the antenna: Turn up the volume to hear his story!

  
  

Rafael Antonio in Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
To tinker, you don’t need to be an expert or have experience in building networks, antennas, or cables. Like Mr. Rafael Antonio, you too can be encouraged to collaborate with others to create a common good.
Currently, the community of San José del Peñón, together with its community, has continued to do SOLE on its own, and using Group Internet to investigate Big Questions such as: Why does water make things wet?, Why don’t humans use 100% of our brains?, Why is there fresh water and salt water?, Why are babies born without teeth?

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).

SOLE led by Ambassadors at SOLE Festivals, Montes de María (2024).
That’s not all, the community of San José del Peñón also created its own website, where they can upload their products and services, share their traditions, games, and everything they want to show the world about their community. Take a look!
SOLE: San José del Peñón

Second Stop:
Since 2023, we have built a super close relationship with the community of La Haya. This year, one of the SOLE Ambassadors from there joined as a SOLE Explorer to help us bring a connectivity solution that she already knew to San José del Peñón. Mariana Fernández was our indispensable support in training new ambassadors in her municipality and managing to install the connectivity solution in this new SOLE community.
Turn up the volume to hear in her own words what this experience was like, and how using the internet in a group has transformed her territory:

  
  

Mariana Fernández, Tuning Visits, Montes de María, (2024).
Thanks to community collaboration and the implementation of solutions like the Rural KIT, today San José del Peñón and La Haya have community Internet access, facilitating both learning and cultural exchange in the Montes de María.

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.title: How did internet improve in Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-nuevomex.content:
Affection, a will for change, and reconciliation? It is being lived in the Nuevo México rural district, the Nasa Kiwe Tekh Kxsaw community located in Santander de Quilichao.

Community research on connectivity, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).

Community analysis process of Internet access, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
Using the SOLE methodology, the community asked themselves what happens to our body when we are hugged? A majority of women using the internet and computers in a group. Laughing, talking, researching through the internet, understanding those things they had never talked about, or had always assumed. Sharing their feelings and creating new knowledge. Together.

Hands-on tinkering and learning at the SOLE Lab, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
How the internet works was the topic addressed in a workshop format: submarine cables that carry the Internet signal along the ocean floor to the community, how to use it together, and what we can do with that great network that unites us on a global scale.
We installed a Jangala and an omnidirectional antenna in a space where the community meets recurrently to make decisions.

Implementation of the Jangala device for community connectivity, Nuevo México, Santander de Quilichao (2024).
Currently, the Nasa Kiwe Tekh Kxsaw community continues to ask themselves Big Questions using the Internet and technology as a group. Let them tell you themselves 👇🏽

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.title: How did internet improve in Piendamó, Cauca?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-piendamo.content:
The USAID and IOM Hilando Vidas y Esperanza (Weaving Lives and Hope) program brought SOLE Colombia to El Agrado. Together, we have worked to bridge the digital divide, bringing Internet access to isolated communities and giving connection a purpose: using the Internet together to learn in a self-organized and autonomous way. Since 2023, Piendamó, Cauca, has been the protagonist of this story of change.
Alexander García, the “Cacharrero” Building Bridges
It was in El Agrado that we met Alexander García, a young community leader with a curious and committed spirit. From the beginning, Alexander was enthusiastic about technology and, especially, the Internet. With the support of SOLE, we installed a connectivity solution and some computers in the community hall, which soon became the center for learning and gathering for his community.

Collective explanation about connectivity and the Internet, Piendamó, Cauca (2023).

Practical demonstration of Internet use during SOLE Festivals, Piendamó (2023).

Children and youth exploring the Internet during SOLE activities, Piendamó (2023).

The Journey to the Misak Pisicatau Reserve
Alexander’s curiosity to understand how routers, antennas, and networks work quickly led him to become an expert. In a matter of months, he went from being someone who didn’t care about technology to a “cacharrero” (a tinkerer/handyman). This newly acquired skill has turned him into a bridge between his community and other neighboring communities, sharing his knowledge with others.
In 2024, Alexander joined us on a new mission: to bring the Internet to a neighboring indigenous community in the Misak Pisicatau Reserve. Upon arrival, we performed speed and signal tests, and it was Alexander who quickly discovered that no antenna could achieve a stable connection in that mountainous region.

  
  

SOLE Tuning Visits, Piendamó, (2024)
The good news is that the Reserve had a stable satellite Internet connection, so we only had to install a router to make it more precise. Listen to him talk about the moment we installed a router with confidence!

  
  

Tuning Visits, Piendamó, (2024).
With his technical skills and passion for teaching, Alexander was the first to motivate the inhabitants of the reserve to explore the possibilities of the Internet and join the SOLE movement. With his support, we installed computers in the community hall, and Alexander encouraged them to continue using Self-Organized Learning in their community. Thanks to his drive, the Misak Pisicatau community has now created its own website, a space where they share their traditions, culture, and knowledge with the world.

Misak Piscitau Reserve, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).

Misak Piscitau Reserve, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).

Misak Piscitau Reserve, Piendamó, Cauca (2024).
This is just one of many stories that demonstrate the power of connectivity to open doors and connect worlds. We invite you to learn more about the activities this community has carried out and the projects they have created on their website.
SOLE: Resguardo Piscitau

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.title: How did internet improve in El Tambo, Cauca?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-tambo.content:
Have you ever imagined a place where an entire community can connect to the Internet, learn, and create together? In El Tambo, Cauca, that dream was a shared necessity.
In this community, Internet connection in rural areas is very limited, and in the urban area, access is mostly private. A public space with Internet became essential for everyone to connect, work on their collective projects, and strengthen their territory.
In 2023, thanks to our partners at ADAPT Peace Building, we met the community of El Tambo and their community circles: the youth circle, the water circle, and the women’s circle. These groups had been working for over a year on peacebuilding and strengthening the social fabric. From that first meeting, a deep connection was created. The circles quickly embraced the SOLE methodology and saw group Internet as a tool to achieve a collective dream: a community space with Internet connection. That was how the spark of the SOLE Lab was ignited in this community.

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).

SOLE Lab, El Tambo, Cauca (2024).
During 2024, the Ambassadors of El Tambo were trained in the SOLE methodology and, together with RUTA 4 Taller, the collective work and the hands of the community brought their own SOLE Lab to life: The Second Library of the Future in Colombia!
This is how one of the neighbors of the SOLE Lab in the Barrio Obrero describes it:

  
  

Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).

  
  

Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
The SOLE Lab is not an ordinary library. It is a meeting point where children, youth, and adults explore, create, dream, and learn together. With access to community Internet and collaboration spaces, the SOLE Lab invites the community to turn ideas into actions, to make collective decisions, to enjoy self-organized group learning, and why not, even watch movies.

  
  
Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
Thanks to the SOLE Lab, the Internet connection in El Tambo improved significantly. Today, anyone can come by and enjoy a more stable and faster connection, allowing students, families, and neighbors to connect, research, and create new ways of using the Internet together.
Now the community of El Tambo can communicate and create bonds with other SOLE Lab communities and people around the world. With each connection, bridges of collaboration are built that strengthen the sense of belonging and collective learning; each participant of the Library of the Future is part of a global network of learning and transformation.

  
  

Plug in Your SOLE Lab in El Tambo, Cauca, (2024).
Check out some of the activities that the community has promoted in this space:

Community participation in the SOLE Lab of El Tambo, Cauca (2024).
Today the SOLE Lab awaits us with open doors to continue building the future of the Internet together!

en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.title: How did internet improve in Valdivia, Antioquia?
en/inspire/insp-internetimprove-valdivia.content:
KM15 is the geographical point on the road leading to the Corregimiento of Puerto Valdivia from the municipal seat. It is also the name of the community settled in this place. Life in Km15—kilometer 15, as it sounds in Spanish—flows along the road that connects it to the rest of the world… or not. Its geographical situation is a metaphor for its digital situation: in many places, the Internet is an everyday thing; there, it feels distant.
Community Internet access was a dream for its inhabitants. Most relied on expensive data plans on their cell phones or satellite Internet, options that are not always accessible and that limit their possibilities.

  
  

Following contact with new ways of using the Internet, through the Hilando Vidas y Esperanza program—from USAID, implemented by IOM and SOLE Colombia—the women of KM15, who had already experienced the power of being able to use the Internet in a group, were drivers of change.
Their commitment to learning led them to tinker and transform that reality. Accompanied by SOLE Colombia, and guided by their enthusiasm and dedication, we managed to install a Jangala device in the community hall: a space that, from one moment to the next, became the connection center of Km15.

  
  


  
  

Tuning Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).
The donation of several computers completed the toolkit with which these Ambassadors can now lead SOLE sessions in their community, bringing their neighbors closer to learning, technology, and a world full of possibilities.
Today, the community hall is not only a meeting place, but also a place to share Internet and to manage resources as a community.

Tuning Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia (2024).

Tuning Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).
The story does not end there. The Ambassadors now understand how the Internet works, why it is important to manage it, and the difference in Internet gigabyte consumption that can exist between watching a movie or sending a message, both in terms of consumption and their economy. Now, they are experts at using computers and the Internet in a group.

  
  

Tuning Visits, KM 15 in Valdivia, Antioquia, (2024).

  
  

Women are taking ownership of Internet use in Valdivia. And you, have you ever wondered why you pay what you pay for your cell phone plan or home Internet?

en/inspire/insp-life-and-technology.title: How can technology help us weave stories?
en/inspire/insp-life-and-technology.content:
Implementation site: Recharge your SOLE LAB in Boca de Camarones
Implementation date:
2023/11/04
Figure 1. Photograph showing the connections made by the participants regarding their life experiences in relation to technology.


Purpose: To recognize each other as part of the SOLE Lab project through our life stories in relation to technology.
Device instructions


Tell your life story through what technology has allowed you to do. To do this, select 3 milestones or relevant moments and draw them in a vignette.


How do our stories connect? We will use yarn to connect everyone’s stories.


Device development

The experiences narrated below are the result of what each participant said about their life experiences in relation to technology. To avoid misrepresentation, we use ““ as a way to quote what the person actually said. In other parts of the text, the person is paraphrased, trying to maintain fidelity to what was expressed throughout the session.
We use the word milestone to refer to those important events or occurrences that are relevant to the person telling them.
The order of the names appearing in this systematization is the order in which the people connected the stories. For example: Óscar started by telling his three milestones. Subsequently, Lizeth from SOLE Colombia, because she connected what she had drawn with one or several of Óscar’s milestones.
There were moments in the session where the speaker connected with the stories of several participants who had already spoken.

Óscar [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “My first television was the first one in the community.”
Milestone 2: “When I gave presentations at school, other people did it with a Video Beam and I did it manually; this made me feel inferior; however, the teachers valued my posters much more because of how creative they were.”
Milestone 3: “I didn’t touch a computer until I was eleven (11) years old. I locked that computer and I was very afraid of technology.”

Lizeth [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: Her father bought a cell phone that became the community’s cell phone.
Milestone 2: The video game machine at her parents’ store allowed her to have more popularity and friends.
Milestone 3: “I filled myself with floppy disks of my favorite series and learned many songs.”

Elainer [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: His first contact with computers was while studying.
Milestone 2: He worked at a Punto Vive Digital and was able to help many people.
Milestone 3: “I found SOLE Colombia and lived the experience of setting up a SOLE LAB in my community.”

Marcelo [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: He supported the Punto Vive Digital where he worked with his brother. He says that in his childhood he knew nothing about technology, as he had not had contact with those “gadgets.”
Milestone 2: He recognizes the moment when the SOLE LAB materials arrived.
Milestone 3: His first cell phone. “My first cell phone broke.”

Sebastián [audiovisual production]:

Milestone 1: “They gave me my first tape recorder. ‘Let the music play!’, he said.”
Milestone 2: “They gave me my first guitar. ‘Let’s make some noise!’, he said.”
Milestone 3: He talked about his first computer and how exciting it was to know everything he could do.

Gustavo [Internet Society Foundation]:

Milestone 1: Since he was little, he liked making magazines. When he was a kid, he started writing a blog. “This was my first job at a digital newspaper.”
Milestone 2: “My first cell phone allowed me to see the world without being afraid of the information I could find.”
Milestone 3: “Video calls allow me to connect with my sister and my nephews.”

Ana María [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “Through the internet, I connect with my friends in Aracataca.”
Milestone 2: “From age 9 to 11, I had my first MP3 player.” She says she has always liked listening to music. “I would take over the remote for our first DVD player and wouldn’t lend it to my siblings.”
Milestone 3: I met Marcelo (her partner) through social media. “He lived in Santa Marta and we couldn’t see each other,” she said.

Mateo [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: He remembers his first heartbreak email. “I was writing to a person I liked, but who didn’t pay attention to me.”
Milestone 2: “My aunt gave me my first analog camera. It had a roll with 20 photographs.”
Milestone 3: “My first computer broke. It was frustrating for my parents, who went into debt.”

Nicolas [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: He was calling a radio station asking for tickets to the Soda Stereo concert. “The station answered me, but the dog took the internet cable and the call to the station was cut off.”
Milestone 2: He remembers his first video game and Game Boy.
Milestone 3: His father taught him how to ride a bicycle.

Caril [Boca de Camarones]:

Milestone 1: “I learned to use a calculator at age 9. I didn’t know how to use it, it scared me, but I learned.”
Milestone 2: She learned to use a laptop. “The internet has been a great tool for learning how to use technology,” she said.
Milestone 3: “Thanks to SOLE, I have gotten into the world of networks and technology. I want to keep learning.”

SanJay [SOLE Colombia]:

Milestone 1: “I bought a sampler to make music.” It gave him a lot of happiness because he felt he could make his own music.
Milestone 2: “At 16, I won a scholarship to study in Hong Kong and I bought a laptop and the movie Matrix on CD. The movie was divided into two parts; my brother scratched CD 2 trying to put it into the DVD player, but it broke and we couldn’t continue watching the movie.” He states that it was frustrating, although now it makes him laugh.
Milestone 3: “I started making my own music.”

Paola [audiovisual production]:

Milestone 1: “They gave me my first camera. It was red. I am nearsighted, but I learned how to use it. I collected many cameras throughout my life because I like to keep the memory of moments.”
Milestone 2: “I remember my first cell phone looked like a brick.”
Milestone 3: “The internet arrived at the house. This gave me the possibility to connect with my friends in Uruguay.”

Findings and learnings

In the session, the participants connected the stories emotionally and intuitively. There was no sense of moral or acquisitive superiority among the stories.
Having to connect with another person’s story keeps everyone in a constant state of listening.
It is interesting how stories appear about the first technological device, be it a television, a cell phone, a printer, etc., as well as how these devices allow new relationships with other people to be generated.
It is interesting how life stories in relation to technology say a lot about who we are and what we have ceased to be today. Many stories connect with people’s passions, tastes, or character traits.
The milestones are related to happy, pleasant stories, but also those that generate shame, pain, or nostalgia.
The importance of these devices lies not in the story itself, but in the way people connect their stories to one another.

en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.title: Trayectoria socio-técnica · Comunidad de Cacharreras
en/inspire/insp-sociotech-cacharreras.content:
We set out to create this divergent space you are exploring called SOLE Voltage: The Solutions Guide for connectivity. In this log, you will find the account of the development of a multiplicity of experiments that we designed and executed with the goal of improving the user experience and interaction with our community of cacharreras (tinkerers). Below, you will find a log organized into macro-events and micro-events, where the account of what happened is unfolded in light of the analytical tool of “socio-technical trajectories.”

Macro-events: These are phases we designed for the development and implementation of SOLE Voltage. They can be seen in the following diagram:



Micro-events: These are the specific significant events that occur in each of the trajectories.
Socio-technical trajectory: A socio-technical trajectory is a process of co-construction of products, production and organizational processes, institutions, user-producer relationships, learning processes, problem-solution relationships, processes of constructing the functionality/non-functionality of a technology, rationalities, policies, and specific strategies. To understand more about socio-technical analysis, you can go to our conceptory.

Stating three major controversies of interest in this trajectory, we have:

The understanding of the controversy related to creating and caring for a community of cacharreras. There are several experiments and concrete actions that allowed for the activation of a certain interest and action in particular users, but which in the end could not be sustained. It seems that, due to the possibilities and limitations of SOLE-Voltage to date, considering the “Cacharrera” as a subjectivity that is maintained over time is very costly. It makes more sense to think of it as specific activations that occur from deployments in events, workshops, or by chance, which will not necessarily permeate over time, but rather that this user will enter the cacharrero logic in very limited times and spaces.
The evolution of user testing showed a broader understanding of it, which allows it to be configured in itself as a deployment of Voltage in which observation and analysis are central. That is to say, it seems that the most appropriate way to deploy Voltage is through a user test, because the very novelty of this guide makes our understanding of appropriation still very short and particularized. If we do not continue in that exercise of praxis and reflection, it will be very difficult to achieve its appropriation.
Two rhetorical and material lines were built that we have not yet synchronized: on one hand, that of SOLElab as the Library of the Future and, on the other, that of Voltage: The Solutions Guide. Due to the ways in which we approached the execution and the complexity of both processes, we only managed to articulate very concrete points of union that did not achieve adequate integration. Although this remained as such at the time of this trajectory’s completion, it is not very clear whether the integration of the two lines is the most appropriate way to allow for the understanding of the appropriation of one virtual space and the other physical space.

Answer: Mind Map as a tool.
Data discrimination based on the concepts:


Life and health (main source for drinking and cooking)


Culture and spirituality (Cultural identity and celebrations)


Sustenance and economy (fishing and food)


Relationship with nature (Traditional knowledge and environmental awareness)


Education and future (community water care projects)



Group 4
Authors:
David Linares
Luis Ortiz
Antonio Diaz
Gabriela Leaño
Herib Campos
What does water mean to you and your community?
We are going to work with two tools, participatory mapping and ethnographic video.
Participatory mapping:
Participatory mapping will work to visualize and understand the social, emotional, and care dynamics regarding the meaning of water for the community. It is a tool for working with the community, through talking circles.
1. Community activation and trust

Meeting with community leaders and key members of the community.
Explain the purpose and ask for permission to document with ethics and consent.

”Support tool: Talking circle + Audiovisual consent form.”
Proposed games and dynamics:
1. The voice of the river (creative presentation dynamic)
Objective: break the ice, introduce yourself, connect with water.
How to play:


Each person introduces themselves by saying their name and completing this sentence:

“If I were water, I would be…” (a waterfall, a calm river, a storm, a happy little puddle, etc.)



Variant: have them do it by imitating the sound or movement of the water they chose.
2. Emotional map of water (on the ground)
Objective: identify emotional bonds.
How to play:

A large circle is drawn on the floor (with tape or branches) as a territory.
The facilitator asks questions such as:

“Where did you feel joy with water?”
“Where were you afraid of water?”
“Where did you learn something important with water?”


People walk and position themselves within the map according to their answer. They can share if they wish.


Material: dry leaves, tape, chalk, stones to mark zones.

2. Ask, feel, and draw (Participatory mapping)
Activity:


In groups, a large poster board is handed out with a silhouette of the territory (it can be free-form, not geographical).


The question is asked:
What does water mean to you?
Where is water present in your daily life?
Where does the water flow? Where does it stop? Where is it missing?


They draw and write:

Rivers, streams, wells, sacred sites, areas of scarcity, memories, uses, threats.
They can also use symbols, words, or emotional colors.


Materials: poster boards, markers, crayons, stickers, printed icons, colored paper.

Ethnographic video
The ethnographic video will help us to identify and keep an external record of the underlying dynamics of behavior and meaning regarding water.
During the mapping:

Film the conversations while they draw.
Interview key people with open-ended questions (children, knowledge keepers, fishermen, women leaders):

What memories do you have of water?
What rituals or stories exist about water?
What has changed in the water of the territory?



Additionally:

Record landscapes, bodies of water, sounds of the environment, daily activities (washing, navigating, collecting).


Recommendation: use close-up shots of hands drawing, faces while speaking, the stroke that grows. That adds great visual and emotional value.

en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.title: Has it happened to you that a video loads faster on someone else's phone?
en/inspire/insp-speed-access-info.content:
We say that the Internet is fast if we can quickly access the information we consult.
Megabytes of download (MB) are a measure of how quickly internet data is transmitted. The more MB you have, the faster your internet is.
If you have:

More than 5 MB: it is a good speed with which you can watch videos, listen to music, and perform different activities on the internet.
Between 1 MB and 5 MB: you can have a stable video call.
Less than 1 MB: you can perform searches on the internet and send text messages.

The more devices that are connected to the internet, the fewer download MB you will have. This happens because the speed is distributed among the number of connected devices.

The photo-textual breakdown
To be a boy, girl, child_, to be anoth_r

When I remember my childhood, I see myself taking toys apart to understand how they worked; sometimes I would reassemble them and they would work, and other times they wouldn’t. I don’t forget a battery-operated police car that would pop out two uniformed officers—gringo style, with a gun in their hand—from each door as it moved forward. This was one of those that, fortunately, I could never reassemble.
Part of my childhood was permeated by the presence of toys; just as this police car existed, I remember taking my soccer ball everywhere. Even when I had the opportunity to see the ocean, I took my futsal ball in my airplane luggage, and fortunately, it didn’t burst. My toys are with me.
Without knowing the world behind it, the naive instinct of a child who only knows what their parents enable allowed me to disassemble structures, just for the sake of curiosity. I didn’t see interest behind the artifacts; I only saw smaller worlds that I wanted to understand, that I wanted to open.
What can bring more enjoyment than a toy? Sometimes just a smooth stone, thrown with the right technique, can bring free moments of enjoyment and memory when approaching a lake.
Being an adult is taking charge of your inner child_. Just as I painted, played, and studied, my identity increasingly returns to its multiple and rhizomatic childhood. Being a “cacharrero” (tinkerer) is sometimes an identity, but now, thanks to Mate, I see that it is also a noun. Sometimes we are tinkerers, and we solve things, other times we don’t. What is it that mobilizes you to tinker?

To have your bag of toys

My bag of toys for the workday. 1. The bag with pockets. 2. The headphones to listen better. 3. The headphone case to protect them. 3. The hard drive to back up information. 3. Pens, cutter, and eraser. 4. The cell phone charger. 5. The toothbrush and toothpaste. 7. The USB drive so I don’t have to work in the cloud and can keep the information close to me. 8. The Game Boy Advance. 9. Pokémon Sapphire.
The carrier bag theory of fiction
Ursula K. Le Guin
1986


Now the full essay:
pdf essay
Retrieved from: mirror.anarhija.net/es.theanarchistlibrary.org/mirror/u/uk/ursula-k-le-guin-la-teoria-de-la-bolsa-de-transporte-de-la-ficcion.pdf
The tinkering kit, the collection of toys and potions

Taking a part of the text “Making Dissent a Politics of Ourselves” by Eric Sadin, I appeal to witchcraft (past), and witches like the powerful Isabelle Stengers, and to science fiction (future) with psychonauts like Aldous Huxley; I invite you tomorrow to create potions together. Just as we used to do the Sabbath, last Saturday as a partial closing, we are going to make our territorial journey and try some of the potions we design tomorrow.
“In the preface to a new 1946 edition of Brave New World, Aldous Huxley writes these words, whose scope and limits should be grasped:

“If I were now to rewrite this book, I would offer the Savage a third alternative. Between the utopian and the primitive horns of this dilemma, there would lie the possibility of sanity, a possibility already realized, to a certain extent, in a community of exiles or refugees from the brave new world, who would live in a kind of Reservation. In this community, the economy would be decentralist and Henry George-style, and the politics, Kropotkinian and cooperative. Science and technology would be employed as if, like the Sabbath, they had been created for man, and not (as at present) that man should be adapted and enslaved to them.”

For now, I only use this fragment to invite you to create potions for the human, for our collectives that empower them, that adapt to them, not that enslave them.

Like Hermione Granger, our trinkets or knick-knacks (magazines, markers, flowers, cables…) can support us in world-building, in our potions. Just as an example, to leave so much poetry behind, the potions can be: activity designs, lists of questions, fanzines, scents that prepare people for something, drawings, poems… in short. Those potions depend on your skills, interests, the communities you wish to care for, and the purpose you envision for a specific time-space.

Also, like Seamus Finnigan, we can have accidents. Ultimately, we are in a perpetual learning process from which we will never have guarantees of what will happen, especially when we are dream-designing alternative worlds. My only call is to care, harm-free action, and precaution as policies. My potions seek to follow these principles by seeing the potential in oneself and in others, in the other, positioning oneself not from fear, but from trust, respect, and co-responsibility. What will be the guiding values for your potions?
