en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.title: En grupo, solucionamos mejor
en/inspire/insp-tinkerer-inspiration.content:
Is having internet a problem for you? In a world where not all of us have internet and where we feel increasingly lonely, there are communities that have come together to answer the Big Questions of life while building connectivity networks that have allowed them to improve their internet and strengthen their community fabric through Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLE). These communities use community antennas, low-cost technologies, and a tinkering and collaborative spirit to overcome barriers and solve connectivity problems that once seemed insurmountable.
What if it is there, in this willingness to solve connectivity problems, that the future of the internet is born? And what if every internet connection were a vital connection between life stories that come together to change the world together? We no longer want to be spectators, but protagonists of our own story.
SOLE Voltaje is not limited to offering easy answers; instead, it poses questions that spark curiosity and empower people to find their own solutions.
These communities show us that, with ingenuity and determination, it is possible to transform connectivity problems or challenges into opportunities. We use the internet in groups because it is safer and because every internet connection is a connection with other people; it is a bond of solidarity and learning.
So, let us celebrate these Colombian communities that are weaving a network of hope through the internet. Their work is a powerful reminder that together we can build a more connected future, where every voice counts and every story finds its place; it is a reminder that another internet is possible. This new way of connecting is just beginning. We call this the Library of the Future.
SOLE Voltaje
When someone faces a connectivity problem, SOLE Voltaje appears with its sparkling energy: “Have you tried restarting the router? It’s like giving your connection a coffee!” But its approach goes beyond simple tricks; it invites everyone to think: “Is your network saturated because everyone is watching cat videos? What if you get together with other people to use the internet as a group? Maybe it’s time to reach agreements on how we want to use the internet.”
Library of the Future
In a corner of the future, there exists a Library that does not depend on books, but on the relationships between people. This is a space where knowledge is not in a specific place, but in the vast network of the internet and the connections it enables between people and communities. Here, the Big Questions of life wait to be explored. This Library of the Future invites us to gather, to share ideas, and to learn together. In every corner, the energy of collaboration is felt: groups of people immerse themselves in deep discussions, using technology not as a barrier, but as a bridge toward understanding. The Library of the Future teaches us that, through connection and dialogue, we can discover answers we had not considered.
In a world where curiosity and technology converge, the Library of the Future has found an unparalleled friend: SOLE Voltaje, a solution guide designed to illuminate the path toward knowledge. Together, they create a vibrant space where the internet is not just a tool, but an ally in the search for the Big Questions of life.

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.title: Prueba #01 SOLE Voltaje
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-test01.content:
Presentation
Hi, I’m Nicolás, the tinkerer at Voltaje. Today we want to share the design of this User Test that we designed and executed at the beginning of 2024. We learned a lot in this process and we would like you to be able to adopt and use them to interact with your communities.
Objective
To evaluate the functionality of three connectivity solutions currently documented on the Voltaje platform.
Solutions
The difficult technique
Installing a web server on a pocket computer.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide

The easy tinkerer way
How to improve my signal with a can?
Estimated duration: 10–15 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide

The easy technique
Restarting and sharing phone internet with other people.
Estimated duration: 10 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide

The difficult tinkerer way
Building a homemade 3G antenna.
Estimated duration: 40–60 minutes.
SOLE – Voltaje · Connectivity solutions guide
Audience
Profile 1 - Doña Marlén, interested (+), skill (-)
She is a person over 50 years old, with a genuine interest in knowing how to use the internet to improve her way of life. She finds it difficult to use a cell phone, a computer, and browse the internet. She is a mother.
Profile 3 – Pepito, interested (-), knowledge (+)
He is a person between 14-21 years old, a student, likes to use social networks, play video games, and is currently studying. He likes to have the latest technological gadgets and is informed about them.
Profile 2 - Paila Gorrea, interested (-), skill (+)
She is a person between 30-40 years old, works with NGOs coordinating projects, and lives between the city and the rural communities she works with. She interacts with large funders to secure funding for NGO projects.
Profile 4 – Juanita, need (+), knowledge (-)
Methodology
VOLTAJE is presented along with some categories of interest to us in relation to its functionality. Then, guests are allowed to read and develop a solution individually, while in parallel, they comment on their observations in relation to the categories presented. The above is repeated with another solution. At the end of the solution, specific questions are asked in relation to the categories of interest, and finally, an open group feedback session will be held.
Observer
Your task is to be present, taking careful notes on how the user develops a solution by reading the instructions. You must be attentive to notice points of boredom and frustration.
Moderator
This is the person who presents and provides direction for the final feedback. Other observers can participate by asking occasional questions, keeping the following recommendations in mind:

They must avoid giving judgments and reflections.
They cannot give opinions about the solutions.

This does not mean they cannot induce answers from people.
Since the central categories are “readability and viability,” the conversation will focus on these. The “accessibility” category may be explored in detail at a time when VOLTAJE is more advanced.
Agenda









































TimeMomentDescriptionTools9:00–9:15Welcome• Thanks for coming, welcome to SOLE• Let’s get to know each other: Name, what you do• (Optional) Tell us about a time you had a problem with the internet and what you did• Where are you located? Profile lines (Knowledge, skill, motivation, and need)SnacksPositional mapsPost-its9:15–9:25Exploration of Voltaje• What do you know about SOLE?• (Optional) Short video about SOLE• Why are you here? (Sanjay)• Connectivity Solutions Guide• Reasons for not having internet: money, signal, knowledge• Connectivity self-management (using internet in a group: learning, cheap, safe, fun)• You will test two prioritized solutions and give feedback• First solution: 20–30 min• Second solution: 40–60 min• Skills are not being evaluated, but the solutions themselves9:25–9:30Presentation of SOLE Voltaje and the exercise• How the Voltaje page is set up• Types of solutions• Meaning of icons• Structure of a solution9:30–11:00Testing the solutions• Device: cell phone or computer• Link sent via WhatsApp• Presentation of the 2 solutions and times• Build a homemade 3G antenna (40–60’)voltaje.solecolombia.org/#Construye%20una%20Antena%203G%20casera• How to improve my signal with a can (10–15’)voltaje.solecolombia.org/#%C2%BF%C3%B3mo%20mejorar%20mi%20se%C3%B1al%20con%20una%20lata%3F• Groups of 2 participants per solution• Observer per guest (takes notes)• The participant can express frustration or blockageEvaluation form11:00–13:00Group feedback• Guided conversation with questions• Listen to participant comments• Take notes in the feedback section
Observation during the test
Instructions:

Before the guest starts working on the solution, explain to them concretely what your role will be and why.
You can hand the evaluation form to the participant once they have finished the solution or have decided to stop.
Tell each participant to take the necessary time and read each of the statements they are going to evaluate carefully.
10 minutes before finishing the test, ask the participant to stop their work and fill out the evaluation.

Observer’s role:

Foster a calm and trusting space for each participant. The observer must not judge what the participant is doing. This should be a companion role.
Take note of the participants’ reactions and behaviors while they work on the solution; without making them uncomfortable, being invasive, or intimidating the participant.
Take note of the questions each participant has and suggest that they do/solve them however they think best; but without extending, helping, or trying to answer their doubts.

Suggestion questions: How would you solve that doubt or problem? What do you think is failing in the explanation or solution for you to have that doubt or problem?

Invite participants to evaluate each of the solutions calmly and honestly. The more objective and critical the participants are, the more profitable the day will be.

If you have any questions about your role as an observer during the test, take note of the question you have. You can only intervene if you see any imminent risk.
Final feedback questions
Reflection on the change in the profile device of interest, knowledge, needs, and skill

Were there changes in how interested you are in tinkering with devices?
Was there a change in how much knowledge you think you have?
Was there a change in how much skill you think you have?
How did you find the experience, how did you feel?
How did you feel?
How was the time?
What did you find most difficult?
What did you find easiest?
What did you learn?
If you were to do this exercise again, what would you change?

Analysis tools
Possible categories (draft)
Under the umbrella of functionality, we can include different categories of our interest; I propose the following, which are recommended qualities when creating instructional texts.











































































ConceptDefinitionQuestionsLegibilityThis concept refers to graphic aspects, typography, color, contrast, text distribution, layout, etc.Is the font type and size easy to read?Do the colors facilitate reading?Is the page layout adequate?Are the images accompanying the texts sufficient or excessive?ReadabilityThis concept refers to the ease with which the text can be read, its clarity, attractiveness, completeness, time, and comprehensibility.Are there ambiguous instructions?Are there incomplete instructions?Do you consider the verb tenses and the wording of the solutions adequate for this instruction?Is the solution complete, or is there a detail missing?I find it difficult to read due to the writing style.StructuringThis concept refers to the order of the sections and, in general, the way the instruction is organized. Its internal logic and the relationship it facilitates for the reader do not waste the reader’s time.Do you think the structure is adequate, or do you think it could be ordered better in another way? Are all sections useful, or do you consider that one is missing or unnecessary?AccessibilityThis concept refers to whether the solutions contemplate multiple ways of receiving information: text, audio, video, image description, etc.Do you consider the solution accessible to different audiences?Do you consider that there is any population group that finds it difficult to access the solution?Do you consider that the solution is presented in such a way that it is accessible to people new to the topic?

If the wording makes reading difficult. |
| Viability | This concept refers to whether the solution can be carried out, if it works; about the resources needed to do it, and if the solution is safe. | Were you able to complete the task that this solution proposed to solve?
Did you find the activity dangerous at any point? |
| Traction | This concept refers to whether the solution sparks the reader’s interest in doing the solution and encourages them to continue developing related solutions. | Did the way the solution is presented encourage you to develop it?
Did the way the solution is presented encourage you to continue developing similar solutions?
Did the way the solution is presented generate interest/motivation for you to continue developing? |
| Learning | This concept refers to whether the instruction allowed you to learn new concepts that allow you to understand how the solution works. | Did you understand how the solution works?
Did you learn new concepts? |
| User test | This is an open category for participants to provide feedback on the exercise design. |  |

Criteria evaluation matrix




















































































































































































































#CriterionStatement12341.1LegibilityI consider the font size and type to be adequate for my reading.1.2The font color and contrast with the background facilitate my reading.1.3The distribution and justification between texts and images facilitate reading and text comprehension.2.1ReadabilityThe way the texts are written facilitates my reading.2.2The texts communicate complete instructions.2.3I know all the words used.3.1StructuringThe order of the instructions is adequate.3.2The number of images accompanying the text is sufficient.3.3The way the instructions are organized allows me to save time.4.1AccessibilityThe instructions are adequate for people new to the topic.4.2The instructions are presented to be used from different devices.4.3The instructions allow access to different types of audiences.The instructions allow me to develop the solution individually and in groups.5.1ViabilityThe instruction allows for developing a solution that works.5.2The materials needed to develop the solution are easily accessible.5.3Do the instructions have any dangerous steps?6.1TractionThe way the solution is presented encourages me to develop it.6.2The way the solution is presented encourages me to learn about other related solutions.6.3The way the solution is presented invites me to know more about this topic.7.1LearningI clearly understood how the solution works.7.2I learned new concepts related to the topic.7.3I can explain to someone how to develop the solution.
Materials





















































#MaterialQty.Link1Ethernet cable (m)1Available in the office.2Quick-drying epoxy glue.5The Sintesolda brand has worked ferreco.com/inicio/6276-adhesivo-epoxico-sintesolda-rapido-transparente.html—CLQ7n5qPA_NQjMA_PR7nAZRoC2WEQAvD_BwE3Plastic cable duct (2 cm)2504Anti-cut gloves2articulo.mercadolibre.com.co/MCO-502525366-guantes-anti-corte-proteccion-trabajo-nitrilo-industriales-_JM#position=6&search_layout=stack&type=item&tracking_id=3c36b974-e272-4bf2-b8c2-692cbf774a855Rigid pole to mount the antenna (a guadua as long as possible, 6 3 meters).36Coaxial cable (m)127Pack of plastic zip ties (10-20 cm)1
Support concepts
Instruction
With the term instructions, I refer to all discourses that order behavior or establish conduct, with imperatives, obligation periphrasis, enumerations of actions, lists of facts, graphic illustrations, etc. Instructions include cooking recipes, traffic codes, contest rules, appliance user manuals, medicine leaflets, employment contracts, or DIY guides. These types of texts govern our lives.
Criteria
Instructions should be:

For everyone. For novices, who know nothing, and for experts, who verify details or solve problems.
Complete and precise: They must cover everything: all functions, all steps, all conditions, or all characteristics of the object or task.
Adequate. It is convenient to order them to “serve” the reader. There are no universal structures or a canonical order. They do not waste time.
Manageable. In addition to being understood, each instruction must be operational. The reader must grasp it with one reading and must be able to execute it without difficulty.
Neutral. Without emotion, courtesy, irony, or humor.
Safe. Confusing instructions can cause accidents.
Comfortable: It is convenient to foresee how the instructions will be used and adapt them to the situation.






























Legibility criteriaExplanation1.1. SizeThe font size should be at least 14 pt.1.2. TextsThe texts should be justified.1.3. ContrastThe contrast should be opposite and facilitate reading.1.4. LayoutThe distribution between texts and images facilitates reading and text comprehension.1.5. TypographyThe course uses accessible typography. Example: Verdana or Trebuchet.

































Readability criteriaExplanation2.1. WritingThe wording of the solution facilitates text comprehension.2.2. ComprehensionThe instructions are easy to understand, regardless of the use of technical language.2.3. MotivationThe wording of the text stimulates and motivates progress in developing the solution.2.4. Course duration and timingThe times for completing the solution are consistent with the instructions.2.5. StructureThe solution instructions are complete.2.6.The solutions need to explain details.
Recommendations
Below are other tips for writing instructions and recommendations:
Give each group of instructions a title. This can be the objective (install a program on the PC), the final product (project budget), or the topic (office etiquette rules). The title allows referring to the instructions in other parts of the text.
Choose the most appropriate terms. These must be precise and also simple so that the reader can understand them. In addition, ambiguous and confusing formulations should be avoided.
Select the appropriate verb form. It is better to use the imperative verb mode, which expresses a command or exhortation, using the “tú” (e.g., avoid terms) or “usted” (e.g., avoid) forms. This way, we address the reader directly. The imperative is clearer than impersonality (e.g., “it is answered”) or the infinitive (e.g., “to answer”). Regarding the form of address (“tú” or “usted”), the Writing Manual points out that this will depend on the degree of formality of the text.

Start with the verb. Starting each instruction with the verb makes the writing clearer. The first thing the reader sees, at the beginning of each line, is what they must do.
Avoid negations whenever possible. These are harder to understand than affirmations. It is better to formulate instructions affirmatively if feasible.
Eliminate repetitions. Reiterating indications should be avoided. It is better to summarize them.
Homogeneity. It is advisable to maintain the chosen writing style in all instructions. For example, it is a mistake to start with a noun—as here, with homogeneity—if a conjugated verb is used in the rest of the instructions. It would be better to say “Write homogeneous instructions.”

Characteristics of an instructional text

The sequence of activities is presented in a correct and understandable chronological order, numbering them and using connectors that help understand the actions to achieve a result.
Graphic marks such as numbers, asterisks, or hyphens are used to differentiate or sequence the series of steps.
It can be accompanied by graphics, illustrations, and/or drawings, depending on the type of instructional text to be developed.
It presents clear, precise, and linear language. It must be understood by anyone.

Guidelines for writing an instructional text

Determine the intention of the text.
Describe the physical resources and functions that make up the action to be performed.
Organize the writing into two parts, headed by a subtitle that identifies its content.
Number each of the steps.
Respect the chronological sequence of the process steps in the writing.
Use verbs in the infinitive, imperative, or 3rd person.
Use chronological connectors: to begin, in the first place, in the second place, finally,
then, after, so, starting from, before, next, immediately, etc.
Add some warnings and precautions that the user should keep in mind.
Use appropriate language according to the activity.
Write with clear and simple sentences.

Resources

www.usability.gov/how-to-and-tools/resources/templates.html
Afilar el lapicero: guía de redacción para profesionales, Daniel Cassany, Editorial Anagrama, 2007.
Recomendaciones_redaccion_instrucciones -IDB, Maria Enriqueta Ponce Ponce
Organization of an instructional text contenidosparaaprender.colombiaaprende.edu.co/G_9/L/SM/SM_L_G09_U02_L07.pdf
How to write precise instructions and recommendations. Writing functional and effective texts in the workplace www.meer.com/es/70130-como-escribir-instrucciones-y-recomendaciones-precisas

Instructions on how to climb a staircase
Julio Cortázar*

No one will have failed to observe that the ground frequently folds in such a way that one part rises at a right angle to the plane of the ground, and then the next part is placed parallel to this plane, to give way to a new perpendicular, a behavior that repeats in a spiral or broken line up to highly variable heights. By crouching down and placing the left hand on one of the vertical parts, and the right on the corresponding horizontal one, one is in momentary possession of a step. Each of these steps, formed as seen by two elements, is situated somewhat higher and further forward than the previous one, a principle that gives meaning to the staircase, since any other combination would produce forms perhaps more beautiful or picturesque, but incapable of moving one from a ground floor to a first floor.
Staircases are climbed facing forward, as backward or sideways they are particularly uncomfortable. The natural attitude consists of standing, arms hanging without effort, head held high, though not so much that the eyes stop seeing the steps immediately above the one being stepped on, and breathing slowly and regularly. To climb a staircase, one begins by lifting that part of the body located on the right below, almost always wrapped in leather or suede, and which, with exceptions, fits exactly on the step. Once said part, which for brevity we will call the foot, is placed on the first step, the equivalent part on the left is picked up (also called the foot, but which is not to be confused with the aforementioned foot), and bringing it to the height of the foot, it is made to follow until it is placed on the second step, with which the foot will rest on this one, and the foot will rest on the first. (The first steps are always the most difficult, until the necessary coordination is acquired. The coincidence of the name between the foot and the foot makes the explanation difficult. Take special care not to lift the foot and the foot at the same time).
Having arrived in this way at the second step, it is enough to repeat the movements alternately until finding the end of the staircase. One exits it easily, with a slight tap of the heel that fixes it in its place, from which it will not move until the moment of descent.

END*

This document aims to outline the protocol for conducting test 02 of the Solutions Guide, based on the learnings and findings from test 01 conducted on 3.02.2024.

What did we learn from test 01?


Focus the drafting of the solutions on improving writing, clarity of language, and the order of instructions.
It is important that the drafting of the solution makes participants feel accompanied in each of the steps.
It is fundamental to understand that the good drafting of steps depends on the strategic use of images, diagrams, or photographs so that they provide key and relevant information.
It is important to focus efforts on improving: 1. the images that accompany each of the instructions; 2. the order, clarity, and organization of the instructions.
It is fundamental to have an initial section with the safety conditions that must be ensured before performing the test.
Before starting the solutions (for the Guide), perhaps tell people that we suggest they be in a comfortable, quiet, and safe space.
Participants said that the solution for the antenna with a can produced more motivation than challenge, and the homemade antenna solution produced more challenge/frustration than motivation. We must review how to manage frustrations.
The tone of the guide should be one of companionship and compassion; a tone in which it is made clear that the solutions are not for experts, that any interested person can do it. This tone is not clear. The ethical and political commitment of the guide should be clear in this tone. There is no clear communicative commitment.
It is worth reviewing which aspects of the typography, font size, and layout facilitated reading. It would be worth testing with people who have difficulty reading on a computer. Also, test layout with column distribution.


Progress: the solutions must make participants feel that they are advancing. Participants must know where they are in the test and how much is left.
Companionship: the solutions must be written in such a way that participants feel accompanied through a colloquial and close tone.
Strategy:
Confirmation: the solutions must assure participants that they are on the right track and that their progress is indeed correct.

Typology of images to be used for the tests

Result images: show the final result of the step or the solution being performed. These images allow participants to contrast the progress they are achieving with what the test asks of them.
Process images: show the steps necessary to reach a result or a specific step.
Context images: show the solutions with people in specific contexts.

Participant profiles
The following profiles can overlap. For example, there are people who may have very little knowledge about how the internet works, but may be very interested in learning for the test.













Interest: people interested in learning how to perform a solution.Need: people who need the solutions to solve concrete problems.Knowledge: people who know a lot about how the internet works, or any of the pillars of the guide: electricity, space, convening people, space management, or connectivity.Skills: people who have soft skills and/or motor skills to perform the solutions.
2. Objectives of test 02:

Evaluate the progress made in the solutions based on the learnings from test 01.
Verify the changes produced in participants by the audio-reading format for the solutions.
Receive feedback on the solutions regarding “how to convene your community” and find the differences and similarities with the “the internet signal is bad” tests:

3. Questions to formulate test 02:

Participant profiles: Based on the learnings and objectives, who and how many people should be part of the test? How do we divide the test for the profiles of interest, need, knowledge, and skills?
Test format: Should we carry out the solution virtually and remotely? What is the reason why we should do it this way? Does remote mean doing the test with a synchronous observer or, on the contrary, giving a time of a week and a half (for example) to perform the test?
Care: What considerations and care should we have for the people who will perform these tests?
Expectations: What do we expect from the people who will perform the test?
Feedback/evaluation: How will we receive the feedback/evaluation from the participants?
Roles: What roles within the SOLE team are necessary to carry out this test?

4. Proposal for test 02 (answers to the questions in point 3):

Participant profiles: Test 02 will be carried out by participants remotely, virtually.


SOLUTION ITERATION TEST: evaluate if the rewriting of the test 01 solutions improved the experience. Two of the participants from test 01 could repeat the tests performed in test 01.

READING TEST with Audio-reading (remote 1 week): With the 4 initial people, both homemade antenna and can.
EXECUTION TEST (remote 1 week): Invite 2 new people to execute the Homemade Antenna test. 2 new people for the can one.


SOLUTION START TEST: verify the progress we have made for people who have not had contact with the Solutions Guide. Two new people could work on one or two solutions different from those prototyped in test 01.

REMOTE 3G antenna installation: 2 Spinning Explorers
IN-PERSON “Restart and share your phone’s internet with others”.


COMPARISON TEST BETWEEN CATEGORIES: verify the necessary changes between the tests on how to “convene your community” and “the internet signal is bad”. The other two participants from test 01 could work on the two new tests on “how to convene your community”.


Test format: Participants will have an estimated time of 1 week and a half to send the results of the test; this will allow us to evaluate, organically, how much interest they had in developing the test.
Care: Since it will be virtual, give people time to perform the test at their own pace. Make people feel calm, comfortable, and be honest with SOLE, both to say they do not want to perform the test and to provide feedback and evaluate the solutions.
Expectations:
Feedback/evaluation:




an entry form (before starting the test) and another one upon finishing the test.


I suggest using the self-documentation method so that, during week 01, people can record their experience with the test.

Common Earth Workshop
Title: Creating devices to reflect on our technological autonomy
Facilitators: Nicolás Gaitán; Manuela Cordoba and Mateo Acosta, Fundación SOLE Colombia
Duration: 90 minutes
Description: First, analog data visualization devices will be installed to foster reflection and dialogue among participants. Following this, we will encourage participants to create their own devices with their own big questions to challenge the rest of the participants.
Objective
To inspire the creation of reflective devices for managing data related to technological autonomy.
Time
1:30 h
Moments

Devices on autonomy, an inspiration (30 min)

Arrival at the space and interaction with the example devices. 5 different devices will be installed to allow participants to reflect on their differences… Additionally, there will be a space with inspirational and problematic references.
Introduction to taking photos.

Device 1 - Colored stones: screen consumption


Question:
How much time do others spend looking at screens?
How much time do you spend looking at screens per day?
Materials: colored stones, spoon, canvas with a circular drawing, baskets to store the stones.


Device 2 - Decision tree: Sharing and privilege

Ideally, everyone should interact in a group with this device. At the end, each person who exits through a path must place a dot.
jamboard.google.com/d/1Y34vGSI9O59fpOe5OWD6ck5qWBsgEy-hZfoSQ56dwbI/viewer


Device 3 - Ladder of technological privileges

Take a step if your power doesn’t go out frequently.
Take a step forward if you don’t usually have difficulty accessing the internet.
Take a step forward if you haven’t felt worried about the amount of gigabytes you consume on the internet.
Take a step forward if you have a postpaid internet plan.
Take a step forward if you have ever bought a cell phone for more than 300 USD.
Take a step forward if you have never had to solve an internet problem on your own.
Take a step forward if you have more computers than the number of people in your house.
Take a step forward if you pay for more than 2 internet services (e.g., Netflix, Spotify, Google Drive, iCloud, Mubi, meditation services, ChatGPT, etc.).
Take a step if you don’t usually spend time in recreational and cultural public spaces.

Materials: Masking tape, printout with the script of the questions.


Device 4 - Ribbons: call to autonomous action


How much of a “tinkerer” (cacharrero) do you consider yourself?
How curious are you to know how the devices you use in your day-to-day life work?
Materials: Colored ribbons, 3 sheets of cardboard.


Device 5 - LEGO data; Awareness-information

If one LEGO brick represents 10 GB, place your assessments in relation to the following questions:

How many GB of internet do you think you consume per month?
How many GB of internet do you think you need?

One person consumes more than 500 GB per month.

www.populoos.es/blog/cuantos-GB-consume-persona-mes/
[www.highspeedinternet.com/es/recursos/cuantos-datos-de-internet-necesitas#:~:text=El%20usuario%20promedio%20de%20internet,un%20informe%20reciente%20de%20OpenVault](www.highspeedinternet.com/es/recursos/cuantos-datos-de-internet-necesitas#:~:text=El usuario promedio de internet,un informe reciente de OpenVault).

Most people need 600 GB per month.
20230606_SOLE+WLH_Prst_Taller de Inspiración SOLE

Library of references

We will leave a section where people can go to consult other ways of presenting data.

Presentation, workshop exhibition, and reflection on the data (15 minutes)

We present SOLE and Voltaje, and the tensions that emerge in our projects regarding data management, and finally, we move with the group of participants to reflect on their answers in the 4 devices.
Reflections
a. Device 1 - Colored stones: screen consumption.
The importance of “tinkering” (cacharrería) for the Latin American context, and how these forms allow an approach to knowledge and local ways of learning.
b. Device 2 - Decision tree: Sharing and privilege
The paradoxes that distance our beliefs from our practices, and the mechanisms to mobilize them.
c. Device 3 - Ladder of privilege: we are positioned from different places and histories, which enables or hinders our becoming on the earth.
d. Device 4 - Ribbons: Estimation of my internet spending
Real estimates of the cost of each type of consumption and national comparison of the prices charged.
e. Device 5 - LEGO data; Awareness-information
Changing habits regarding access to information online and offline, new logics of cultural consumption.
General: Reflection, dialogue, and questioning VS extraction.

Design of your own devices (30 minutes)



Two truths and a lie regarding technology (10 minutes)
People will say two truths and one lie regarding technology, and the others will have to guess which one is the lie.


Design of devices (20 minutes)


Design a quick device to challenge, reflect, and dialogue about the use of technology both in your personal life and in the organizations where you work. Think of questions that the rest of the participants can answer and that can generate great conversations and new questions about it.

Quick exhibition of the created devices and the defined questions.
Invitation to participants to interact with these devices throughout the day.
We close with a general reflection and a thank you.

Economy of resources
The particularity of a reflective VS extractive question
The power of visualization in questioning our habits, beliefs, expectations, etc.

Chatbox Station
DESCRIPTION
Could we propose a relationship with a Chatbot beyond inputs and outputs? Could a Chatbot, from now on Chatbox, invite us to discover the internet in a way that not even the Chatbox itself can anticipate?
With this station, we want to invite participants to discover the possibilities that SOLE Voltaje has and the tinkering spirit through circulation around the space. On the other hand, it is a provocation to reflect on those relationships between humans that machines cannot anticipate.
Phases

Depending on where people stand, an infrared sensor with Arduino will produce sounds and effects that invite participants to explore the space with respect to the place where they are standing.

ChatTinkering Station
DESCRIPTION
How do we realize that we are not alone in this tinkering business? How do we accompany and support each other in the exploration of solutions to improve our experience of using the Internet in a group?
The WhatsApp chat is a place for people who are having connectivity challenges or who are building Voltaje solutions to:

find a community that helps them get through the specific difficulties they have
be able to share/receive new solutions that are not in Voltaje
share/receive how in other places they are using solutions that may or may not be in Voltaje (for example, “5 tricks for…” or other content that we can find on the internet and see how people react) - watch out at the end, the invitation is to use the internet in a group
share/receive interesting information about connectivity challenges and solutions in the world, discoveries, work in other places, initiatives…
provide support to those who venture to explore the Voltaje space, and the test, and find themselves lost - helper?

The purpose of the activity is to observe how the people who participate in the challenges interact with this channel, analyze if it is important and useful for them, and receive feedback on the interaction that develops that day to make the constructions and/or modifications required to fulfill its mission, and provide support among everyone to the people who interact with Voltaje and the test.”
PHASES
Purpose:
Experience the use of the WhatsApp chat to share and discuss connectivity solutions. Each challenge lasts 30 minutes and the challenges can take place at the same time as the participants interact with the rest of the installation activities. There is a group that starts at this station and is in charge of starting challenge 1; after 30 minutes, we notify the next group to start challenge 2 (the same is repeated with 3).
Activities:
The presentation of each challenge is done by Bel through the WhatsApp group

Challenge 1 (30 minutes): The group in charge of the challenge must decide among all the presentation entries which connectivity challenge they find coolest. The discussion takes place live (between the people interacting in this group) and in the chat, with the people who are not at the location. Also, people who are at other stations can participate in the discussion, but those who facilitate or direct this challenge are those in the starting group. In the chat, it must be clear which connectivity challenge they choose to solve.
Challenge 2 (30 minutes): The group in charge of Challenge 2 must find the solution for the challenge proposed in the first challenge, consulting the SOLE Voltaje guide and what they have experienced in the rest of the space. The discussion must be reflected in the chat and the decision of which solution is the most appropriate must be clear to all members of the chat. They can request opinions and experiences from all members. The tinkerers in the chat can stimulate the discussion and can also encourage the exploration of the space in the workshop, or experimentation in the other stations.
Challenge 3 (30 minutes): the group in charge picks up the baton from the previous group (must understand it by reading the chat) and selects the interactions in the chat that they found especially useful or interesting. Then, they must analyze how the chat structure (such as message organization, type of responses, use of multimedia) contributed to the understanding and resolution of the problem.”

en/inspire/insp-voltaje-tests.title: We're building a platform with lots of Voltage, will you join us?
en/inspire/insp-voltaje-tests.content:
Voltaje tests have served us to explore, evaluate, and push further the solutions and devices we have developed to awaken the “cacharrero” (tinkering) spirit and foster an approach to technology and connectivity that leads us to generate spaces for autonomous and community learning.
Thanks to everyone who has participated with us in these tests, we have been able to continue creating ways to extend the blanket of the internet to many places and communities. Furthermore, we have been able to better understand what it is that we do at Voltaje.

en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.title: What is the Internet?
en/inspire/insp-what-is-internet.content:
Download this Inspiration to use it offline
When you think of the Internet, what is the first thing that comes to mind?
If we think of libraries as a repository of human knowledge written in books; that today computers have that information and much more is stored as zeros and ones in their memory; then, we could imagine the Internet as the sum of all the information that is created and saved on all the computers on the planet that are connected through a network of cables and wireless signals and that can exchange that information with each other.
The Internet is much more than that, but in short: it is a large decentralized network of computers that communicate with each other.
There are other communication networks in the world, for example, postal mail, telephony, radio, or television. A big difference between these and the Internet is that on the Internet, people can communicate in both directions and exchange digital information very quickly - at the speed of light!

en/inspire/insp-who-is-solecolombia.title: SOLE Colombia: Who are we?
en/inspire/insp-who-is-solecolombia.content:
At SOLE Colombia, we are creating an equitable and beautiful future together, one Big Question at a time.
We ignite the curiosity of groups of people, transforming internet-enabled spaces into Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLE), to recognize our power and help our lives and communities flourish.
We shake up the status quo by creating communities that learn beyond borders and differences, building bridges between people and ideas, toward a more vibrant shared world.
We are changing the world together!

en/new-here.title: ¿Nuevo aquí?
en/new-here.content:
New here?
Welcome to SOLE Voltaje! An initiative by SOLE Colombia dedicated to improving access to knowledge through community solutions for using the Internet in groups. There are three steps to start using SOLE Voltaje:

Get Inspired: Explore our provocative questions, videos, and stories from the communities we have worked with.
Solve: Find a solution that helps increase connectivity in your place, your community, or your region. The solutions are organized into categories of signal, electricity, devices, people, and space, because to use the internet in a group, you need more than just connectivity.
Have questions?: Share what you learn, write to us with your questions, join our “cacharreros” (tinkerers) WhatsApp group, and help build this movement for a more inclusive internet.

You also have an experience to learn what the Internet is and how it works, and an invitation to help us extend the blanket of solidarity so that others can also get connected: SOLE Voltaje Disconnected.
Our “Cacharrero” Ethics

  
  


SOLE Colombia, 2024

Have you ever wondered how the Internet reaches your home? Why do we pay so much to connect, or what would it be like to live disconnected? Connecting to the Internet might seem like magic, but in reality, it is information traveling the world through servers—physical places that make it possible for you to read this right now.
For many, the “connected” world remains a mystery, either because they lack access or because they don’t know how it works. But here, we like to question everything. We don’t get carried away by the mystery; this is a safe space to explore. Together, we can understand, question, and reinvent the future of the Internet.
SOLE Voltaje is that constant tension between what we already know and what remains to be discovered, between the need to be connected and the desire for freedom and technological autonomy. Here, we develop tools, provocative ideas, inspirations, and spaces for collective learning that promote the use of the Internet in groups to answer Big Questions, because we believe in another possible future for network connection: one that is open, secure, and where we can all decide how we want to be connected—humanly connected.
Everything you find here is the result of the collaboration and knowledge of “cacharreras/os”—as we call them in Colombia—people who do not accept “it doesn’t work” as an answer, people willing to solve, to take apart what no longer works until it functions again. We want more people in the world to be encouraged to build the Internet with their own hands. You, too, can be an active network “cacharrera”!
To change the world together
The goal of SOLE Voltaje is to allow people or organizations working with those who have no access or limited access to the Internet to improve their situation in a self-managed way, as far as their own resources allow.
These resources include the amount of money they can dedicate to improving their situation, the amount of time they have to self-learn, implement, and test solutions, the number of people who could accompany them on their journey, and the level of complexity of the solutions they can develop.
Over time, we hope that people in rural areas and digitally excluded communities can use and link various solutions together to finally have a permanent community space with connectivity and devices to learn, dialogue, and create flourishing communities using the Internet.
There is also a pedagogical purpose behind this guide to invite people to use technology, in a broad sense, to learn.
We would like to re-engage current users and invite new ones to be curious about the Internet and how it works, and how they can use it in a group to learn what they need or are interested in. That is why, within the solutions, there is also a conceptory of terms that teaches users technical and non-technical concepts so they can become active Internet “cacharreros.”
What is SOLE Colombia?
SOLE Colombia is a non-profit organization whose purpose is to create an equitable and beautiful future together, one Big Question at a time.
We ignite the curiosity of groups of people, transforming spaces enabled for the Internet into Self-Organized Learning Environments (SOLE), to recognize our power and allow our lives and communities to flourish.
We shake up the status quo by creating networks of communities that learn beyond borders and differences, building bridges between people and ideas toward a more vibrant shared world.
Did you get started?
If you want to know more about our organization and how we are changing the world, visit our website here.

en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.title: How to partner with others who support your call to action?
en/solve/solv-ally-with-places.content:
Partnering with more visible entities
Hi, I’m Belén. I don’t know much about technology, but I love people and I’m very good at building relationships with them. I arrived at SOLE some time ago and I have learned a lot about the power of people and what we can achieve when we come together.
What does it mean to partner with places that convene?
There are many people and organizations that can make your message reach further and clearer, and that can make your projects a path for transformation in your community. Knowing how to reach them and get their attention is a way to join forces to achieve great things.

What is it for?
Often, you want to count on your community to do things, or learn together, and you find it difficult to find people to join the movement, or you end up doing things with the same people.
With these recommendations, you can learn how to approach others so they support the call to action in your community.

What do you need?

Courage
Curiosity and listening skills
Something to take notes with


How to do it?

Step 1 → Define the purpose of the call. It will be easier to find allies

The first thing is always the reason why you are going to do what you are going to do. If you intend to partner with others, you must be clear about the purpose of what you are going to do with them; only then will you be able to focus well on the search for those who can help you convene.
For example, if you are looking for people to build an antenna, would it be better if you look for them in a hardware store, during the workday, or at the exit of a kindergarten? Perhaps it is a better place where people go to find materials to build things, or tinker. The owner of the hardware store might be a better ally than the school teachers for the call to build an antenna.
Although you should not underestimate the talent of your community, you can prioritize the people and places you want to convene with a ‘why’ that is very clear.
If you can, define your proposal in detail: is it an event, or a series of events? What do you need to have, or buy, or what do you need to equip your purpose with? Do you need to count on more people, or are you going to do it alone?


Step 2 → Locate those who convene, who they are and what they do

Look around you: in your neighborhood, in your community, in your town… you might even have allies in your own home!
Recognizing people and organizations with the capacity to convene, and partnering with them, is strategic to achieving what we want.
Think of people and places where there is a flow of people, people who talk to the community, think of those who organize events. These types of actors will be relevant for convening… keep your purpose in mind so you can better see who has contact with the people you want to convene.
It is worth asking ourselves how we can build networks to achieve a successful call to our activities. If you work on consolidating your skills to join forces with others, you will start to see how it flows better and better for you.

Photo: SOLE Colombia


Step 3 → Read the interests of those who convene and how they resemble yours

Just as you want to organize a specific event, for example, holding a SOLE, other people also have specific interests in the activities they want to promote.
Think about what catches the attention of each of these actors and how you can address both their interests and yours: including the other in a negotiated agenda can win you a long-term ally, and not just a momentary collaborator.
For example, if your interest is to create the habit of holding SOLEs in your community, you can partner with the Local Action Board (JAL). Understanding how to use the Internet as a group to learn things together can meet the JAL’s objectives related to the planning and execution of community development projects, or the guarantee of digital rights for the community; it is a nice way to open the conversation about the activity you want to organize and how the JAL can support the call for your event.


Step 4 → Choose who you want to do what with

Now that you have recognized the strategic actors to convene, and you know how to align their objectives with yours, choose the one you feel most comfortable working with for each of the objectives you have.

Photo: SOLE Colombia


Step 5 → Work on the invitation and the message you want to share

Propose your ideas and prioritize them. Developing each of the ideas you have in a deep way and finding the best way to present them to your ally is a way to practice your speech and the way in which the information can reach them best.
You can make a script of the possible questions and answers that may arise in the conversation. Put yourself in all possible scenarios, take into account the objections and problems that your ally may have regarding your proposal. Having most of the scenarios contemplated, with a possible answer or alternative solution, will make your proposal look strong and consolidated.
Proposing a meeting to show your ideas with order and calm is an excellent way to guarantee the attention of your potential ally. Agree with the person or people who can give a ‘yes’ to your proposal, be punctual for that appointment, and prepare the meeting well.
Work on the order in which you are going to present the information: a careful and orderly speech will let your interlocutor know that you are clear about what you want to do and will give them confidence in counting on you.
Don’t forget to make it very clear:

what you are inviting your ally to
what you will do and what you need from your ally
when you need it
for how long
who will be involved
how communication will be between you
how you are going to tell them what you have achieved thanks to the relationship that unites you




Step 6 → Find out how you can make your proposal

Some allies may be available to you at any time and place. Others have a more formal way of working, or need to make decisions by consensus. Others, even, need you to send a written document with your proposal before you can talk to someone.
Approach the person, organization, business, or any other ally and find out what the best way to present your proposal is. Follow the instructions and organize your time to be able to respond to the requirements on time.


Step 7 → Present your proposal and listen to your counterpart, the goal is to reach an agreement**

It’s time to show everything you’ve worked on! Trust yourself and the rigor with which you have prepared your proposal; we are sure that at this moment, with all the information you have, you will find the words to tell a good story that hooks your ally into doing things together.
Once you have stated your point, listen carefully to your potential ally. There may be information you haven’t considered, so take note of the points that are weak or need to be expanded.
It is also possible that there will be a moment of negotiation: you and your ally should have a scenario where both can win. Open your eyes and ears to anything that might have value for their purpose and strive to create a solid relationship.


Step 8 → Formalize the commitments and let’s get to work!

The moment your potential ally has everything clear and so do you, it’s time to agree and clarify the next steps!
Leave in writing what each one commits to and what the next steps are; it is always better that nothing is forgotten.
Thank the people who have attended to you; starting to work together is just the beginning, and celebrating having reached agreements is a way to honor this new relationship.

Other possible internets
You will know that you have been successful in contacting places that convene the moment you start speaking the same language and find common ground in the conversation.
For example, when someone who can convene others pays attention to the proposal you present and wants you to meet their manager, or a colleague who can help you convene people. Or also, when you find yourself adapting what you are going to say to the interest of the person who is listening to you, creating a space where the ideas start to belong to both of you.
If you exercise your listening skills, you will soon be recognizing people with the capacity to convene and seeking to interest them.
If your purpose is to do a SOLE, you can start thinking about your Self-Organized Learning Environment as a place where several allies can start to fulfill their purposes thanks to your space, or, conversely, you can think of your ally’s space as a SOLE and benefit the people your ally convenes so that they learn to use the Internet as a group to live better together.
You can SOLE any activity or space!

What can you achieve with this solution?
These recommendations are simple and limited. When you go to look for allies, a large part will depend on your communication skills.
Remember that you will not always manage to convince everyone to work with you; the important thing is to do it many times: ‘practice makes perfect’. And, at the same time, listen to your intuition to start creating a ‘radar’ in yourself that warns you of people who can be your allies… stay alert!

en/solve/solv-bandwidth.title: How to make the most of your bandwidth?
en/solve/solv-bandwidth.content:
Take advantage of your Internet service options
Hi, I’m Manu. I’m not a tech expert, but I know how frustrating it is when a movie freezes or a video call cuts out. So, after doing some research, I found a few tricks to improve the connection at home that I want to share with you.

What is taking advantage of bandwidth?
Taking advantage of the options for the internet connection service you have is related to using all the available settings and tools to optimize your online experience in terms of performance, speed, security, and data efficiency.

What is it for?
Did you know that in the world of the Internet, there are two terms that are often confused? I’m talking about bandwidth and speed. Let’s break them down, and I’ll give you some tips so you can get the most out of the bandwidth and speed contracted in your home Internet service.
Bandwidth and speed: what is that?
Imagine that bandwidth → is like a giant cargo truck, so it can carry a lot of packages (data) at once.
The bigger the truck, the more packages it can transport. But here is the key: speed is the time it takes for that truck to reach its destination. So, even if you have a huge truck (high bandwidth), if it doesn’t go fast, the packages will be left waiting!
In conclusion: A high bandwidth allows you to move a lot of data at the same time, but if the speed is low, that data will take a while to arrive. And that is what can frustrate us when we are trying to watch a video or make a video call!

What do you need?

Have a WiFi → Internet service at home.
Patience and curiosity.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Use a network cable

If you can, connect your computer to the Router → with a network cable →. This is like switching from a truck to a high-speed train. The difference is impressive! A wired connection will give you maximum speed and stability.

Photo taken from Pexels, (2024).


Step 2 → Connect to 5GHz if you use Wi-Fi


Screenshot taken by Manuela Córdoba, (2024).
If you cannot use a cable, the next best option is to connect to the 5GHz band of your router. This is like having access to a faster lane on a highway: less traffic, more speed. Just keep in mind that it works best when you are close to the router.


Step 3 → Moment 3: Don’t Forget 2.4GHz

If you are a bit far from the router and you see that the connection is getting slow, switch to the 2.4GHz band. Although it is a bit slower than 5GHz, it can be more reliable. Imagine it is a country road that is always available, even if it isn’t as fast.

Photo taken from Google Photos, (2024).


Step 4 → Adjust the Wi-Fi Channel

Sometimes, the connection feels slow because there are many people in your neighborhood using the same Wi-Fi channel. Changing the channel can make your connection faster and smoother. It’s like moving your party to a place where there is less noise.
Go to Improve your Router’s signal to follow the step-by-step guide


Step 5 → Keep Your Router in Shape

Finally, make sure your router is well-placed and updated. Place it in a ventilated area away from other devices that may interfere. A well-maintained router is key to having a good connection.

Photo taken by Manuela Córdoba, (2024).

How to know if this solution works?
If you checked your speed, your network configuration, and the data consumption on your devices and they are consistent with the data in your contract with your service provider, you can be sure that you are making the most of your Internet service features.
By following these steps, you will not only better understand bandwidth and speed, but you will also be able to optimize your connection and enjoy your online activities without problems.

Why might this solution work?
To ensure that you are making the most of your service features, in addition to checking the speed and bandwidth, you can perform tests at different times of the day; sometimes speeds can vary according to general network saturation.
You can also monitor your data consumption, the data usage of the applications and programs you use, and set some limits to make your consumption more consistent.

en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.title: How to generate electricity using a bicycle?
en/solve/solv-bicigenerator.content:
Hi, I’m Nicolás. I’m what you might call a tinkerer. I’m an engineer and I’m interested in how things work. I enjoy assembling and disassembling devices to understand their inner workings, and I also enjoy figuring out how we can use available resources as a community.
What is a bicycle generator?
A bicycle generator is a system that converts the mechanical energy of a bicycle into electrical energy. Basically, it transforms the pedaling motion into electricity, allowing you to generate power for different purposes, such as charging electronic devices or even powering lighting systems. (Source: Ecologismos)

What is it for?
This solution is a step-by-step guide on how to buy and assemble a bicycle-powered electricity system. We calculated it so that a computer and a router can run for 3 hours, which is the typical duration of a SOLE session.

What do you need?

Money to buy batteries, cables, a power inverter, and a controller.
Energy to pedal.
An old bicycle.
Care and plenty of enthusiasm to assemble the system.
A stand to make the bicycle stationary.


How to do it?

Step 1 → Calculate energy expenditure

Read the energy consumption I need. In this case, we need to power a laptop and a router for 3 hours. This will define the capacity our system must have and the number of hours we must pedal to generate the necessary electricity.

A laptop consumes 120W/h
A router consumes 15W/h

Now, we must calculate the energy expenditure required for the system. You can check this information on the back of the devices or on their chargers. For a SOLE, for example, 3 hours are necessary:

Laptop: 120W/h consumption for 3 hours is 360W
Router: 15W/h consumption for 3 hours is 45W

The sum of these two is 405W over 3 hours. If we divide 405/3h, we get 135 W/h.
The bike machine will be able to generate up to 200 watts/hour pedaling at a medium speed and up to 400 watts/hour at a high speed.



Step 2 → Estimate the characteristics of the complementary equipment.

Remember that to assemble any electricity generation system, you need these components:
An electricity generator
It is any device capable of capturing and transforming some type of energy (mechanical, solar, thermal, hydraulic, chemical) into electrical energy. In this case, it is the bicycle combined with an electric motor and a static stand, but we can also think of a gasoline generator, a solar panel, a Pelton turbine, a wind turbine, etc.



A charge controller
Its function is to regulate the flow of energy going from the motor to the batteries, controlling both intensity and voltage. This is to ensure that the recharge happens under optimal conditions, does not damage the batteries, and extends their useful life.

A battery
It stores the generated energy in the form of chemical energy and releases it later as direct current in a controlled manner.

A power inverter
It converts the direct current coming out of the battery into alternating current so we can plug in our equipment.

Solar cable and accessories
It is an electrical cable robust enough to transmit the electrical energy we generate. Additionally, we can buy plastic connectors that help make the connections more robust and prevent them from disconnecting easily.

As you can see, you can use the same complementary system as you would for a solar panel assembly. For this reason, we will calculate the equipment as if it were for our solar panel system, since they will have the same capacity.


Step 3 → How to estimate battery characteristics?

We had talked about an energy consumption of 405W in 3 hours or 135 W/h. In addition to the total daily consumption, we need:

Days of autonomy (days): This refers to the days of use; if it is used every day, the days of autonomy is 5 or more days, and if it is only used on weekends, we have 1 or 2 days. For our SOLE case, we will set it to a day and a half, 1.5.
Depth of discharge (Pd): For gel or AGM batteries, this value is 70%. For open lead-acid batteries, it is 50%.
Battery voltage (V): We choose this; since our devices are 12V, it will be this value.
Temperature and performance losses: We will assume 15%.

To calculate the battery capacity in Ampere-hours (Ah), we use the following formula: Ah = 1.15 * (Wh/day * days) / (Pd * V) = 1.15 * (135 * 1.5) / (70% * 12) = 27.72Ah. This is the minimum necessary capacity, so we decide to buy a 12V, 35Ah battery.



Step 4 → How to estimate controller characteristics?

For this, we have to calculate the input and output current of the controller, according to these two equations:

To calculate the input current, we just have to multiply 3 values: *1.25: A safety factor of 1.25 is used to calculate with 25% more than necessary to avoid errors due to a very tight calculation. It is a common practice in engineering to oversize calculations by safety parameters in case of failure. *Imod,sc: Unit current of the photovoltaic panel under short-circuit conditions, which can be found on the back of the panel. For this case, it is 2.32 A.

Np: number of panels in series. For this case, there are 2.
Calculating, we have: Iinput = 1.25 * 2.32 A * 2 = 5.8 A. To calculate the output current, we have to add, multiply, and divide the following values:

1.25: A safety factor of 1.25 is used to calculate with 25% more than necessary to avoid errors due to a very tight calculation. It is a common practice in engineering to oversize calculations by safety parameters in case of failure.
Pdc: Direct current discharge power, which is the sum of the current of the devices that we are going to connect and that run on direct current. In this case, we have none, so it is 0.
Pac: Alternating current load power, which is the sum of the current of the devices that we are going to connect and that run on alternating current. In this case, a laptop consumes 120W/h and a router consumes 15W/h, for a total of 135 W/h.
Ninv: Inverter efficiency, around 90-95%.
Vbat: Battery voltage. We can read this on the selected battery. For this case, it is 12V.

Calculating, we have: Ioutput = 1.25 * (0 + (120 + 15) / 0.95) / 12 = 14.80 A. Finally, we just have to round our calculations. Iinput = 5.8 ≃ 6A. Ioutput = 14.80 ≃ 15A. So our controller should support at least an input intensity of 6A and an output intensity of 15A. That is why we bought a 20A one with a voltage of 12/24V (it changes automatically).


Step 5 → How to estimate inverter characteristics?

Since we are going to use low-consumption equipment, the inverter to use is a modified sine wave one. The calculation is done by oversizing 25% more than our total consumption. Remember that the total consumption is 405W. Thus, I = V * 1.25 = 405 * 1.25 = 506.25 W. This should be the minimum capacity of the inverter. In our case, we bought a 750W one.


Step 6 → How to know which cable to buy?

Usually, solar cables are sized using the term AWG (American Wire Gauge) in order to estimate the gauge scale. But for solar cables, the gauge is normally specified by its cross-section or area in mm². Thus, in Colombia, we can find from 2.5mm² to 16mm² gauges depending on the manufacturer.

It should be chosen in relation to the current to be transported. In this case, we will not transport more than 20A, so a 14 AWG cable, that is, 2.5 mm², is fine. Regarding connectors for our case, we bought two, but it will depend on the configuration each person builds.


Step 7 → Find a supplier

Look for a supplier of electrical supplies and get a quote for this equipment. Additionally, you can get advice from them to know if the calculations you made are correct or if there is any other way to optimize your energy generation system. Compare costs between different suppliers and buy taking into account the reliability of the place, the warranty, and the prices.

How to use it?
Precautions
Now that we have the motor, the bicycle, the battery, and the inverter, we must remember that the battery is the last thing to be connected.
A safety warning: We should only connect one of the poles at a time so that we don’t get shocked. It is good to work with rubber gloves as they insulate us from possible electrocution. We recommend reading the section Basic precautions when working with electricity.
Connecting the circuit
The motor has a negative and a positive pole; it is important to identify which is which to build the new circuit. Generally, the positive is represented by red and the negative by black. In the case of connecting a motor, you must identify which way it turns when connected one way or the other; the motor must be connected in such a way that it turns in the same direction that the bicycle will turn, that is, “forward.” Remember that for this solution, what we are doing is running a motor in reverse; that is, by making the motor turn, an electromagnetic field will be created that will interact with the permanent magnets of the electric motor, generating an electric current.

Now, connect the negative and positive cables coming out of the motor to the controller; on this, it is clearly marked where each cable is connected. Then cut two cables and strip their ends to make the connection to the battery.

Now connect these cables coming out of the controller to the battery, respecting the positive and negative connection.

When you have connected them, join the inverter cables to the battery, and that is how you will have your system ready. Once the entire system is assembled, you will be able to connect the computer or the router to the inverter.

Other possible internets
With this solution, you will manage to have electricity to power your SOLE; remember that this solution is calculated with the example of the electrical consumption of a router and a computer. If you want to have permanent electricity for more equipment, you must do your own calculations.

Why might this solution work?
This solution only allows for energy independence for a router and a laptop for 3 hours at night, in case the panel has captured sunlight throughout the day. If you are using it during the day, this time can be extended, since the panel will be charging constantly while you use the electrical devices and it discharges.
